Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 40, verse 1–6 (part 1 of 2):

(Surat Ghafir)
Eighty-five verses, Meccan
In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ha Mim.
The revelation of the Book from God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing,
the Forgiver of sin, the Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty. There is no god but Him; to Him is the final return.
None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve, so let not their coming and going throughout the land deceive you.
The people of Noah denied before them, and so did the factions after them. Every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him, and they argued with falsehood to refute thereby the truth, so I seized them. Then how was My punishment!
Thus the word of your Lord has come true against those who disbelieve: that they are the companions of the Fire.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Ha Mim.
The revelation of the Book from God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing,
the Forgiver of sin, the Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty. There is no god but Him; to Him is the final return.
None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve, so let not their coming and going throughout the land deceive you.
The people of Noah denied before them, and so did the factions after them. Every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him, and they argued with falsehood to refute thereby the truth, so I seized them. Then how was My punishment!
Thus the word of your Lord has come true against those who disbelieve: that they are the companions of the Fire.

Know that there are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, and Hamza and al-Kisa'i, read "Ha" (ḥāʾ) with a kasra (ḥā), while the rest read it with a fatha (ḥa). Nafi' in some transmissions and Ibn 'Amir read it between fatha and kasra, meaning that they do not pronounce it with a full fatha. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it was read with fatha and with sukun on the mim. The reason for fatha is movement to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn) and preference for the lightest vowels, like ayna and kayfa; or it is in the accusative by implying "read" (iqra'). Its non-declension (man' al-sarf) is either due to feminine gender and definiteness, since it is a name of the surah and is definite, and because it is of the pattern of a foreign name like Qabil and Habil. As for sukun, it is because we have explained that names are mentioned in their pausal form.

Page 24
The second issue: The exhaustive discussion of these opening letters is mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. The closer view here is that one says: "Ha Mim" is the name of the surah. So His saying "Ha Mim" is a subject (mubtada'), and His saying "The revelation of the Book from God" is the predicate (khabar). The implied meaning is that this surah called Ha Mim is the revelation of the Book. So "tanzil" is a verbal noun (masdar), but what is meant by it is the thing revealed (munazzal).

* * *

As for His saying "from God": know that when He mentioned that "Ha Mim, the revelation of the Book," it became necessary to explain who the One who revealed it is. So He said "from God." Then He explained that God, Exalted, is described with attributes of majesty and marks of greatness, so that this would move one to exert full effort when listening and would restrain one from negligence and slackness in it. So He explained that the Revealer is "God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing."

Know that people differ concerning what knowledge of God is. A great group said: it is knowledge that He is capable, and after that knowledge that He is knowing. Once you know this, we say: "al-'Aziz" has two interpretations. The first: the Overpowering, so its meaning is the Capable whom no one equals in power. The second: the One who has no like. It is not permissible that "al-'Aziz" here means the Capable, because His saying "Allah" already indicates His being capable, so "al-'Aziz" must be understood in the second sense, which is the One who has no like. And whatever is like this must not be a body, and whatever is not a body is free from appetite and aversion, and whatever is like that is free from need. As for "al-'Alim," it is an intensive form for knowledge, and complete intensiveness is realized only when He, Exalted, knows all things known. So His saying "from God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing" returns in meaning to: this Book is a revelation from the Absolutely Capable, the Absolutely Self-Sufficient, the Absolutely Knowing. Whoever is like this knows the aspects of benefit and harm, and knows that He is independent of attracting benefits and repelling harms. Whoever is like this is merciful and generous, and His actions are wisdom and rightness, free from ugliness and falsehood. So it is as if He, glorified is He, mentioned these three names after His saying "revelation" only because they indicate that His actions are wisdom and rightness, and when this is so, it follows that this revelation is truth and rightness.

It has also been said: the benefit in mentioning "al-'Aziz al-'Alim" is twofold. The first: by His power and knowledge He sent down the Qur'an in this measure which contains benefits and inimitability, and were He not Mighty and All-Knowing, this would not be valid. The second: He undertook its preservation, the generality of the obligation in it, and its manifestation until the end of obligation, and this is not complete except by His being Mighty, who is not overcome, and by His being All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden. Then He described Himself with what combines promise and threat, fear and hope, saying: "the Forgiver of sin, the Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty. There is no god but Him; to Him is the final return." These are six kinds of attributes:

The first attribute: His saying "the Forgiver of sin." Al-Jubba'i said: its meaning is that He is the Forgiver of sin when He deserves forgiveness, either through repentance or through a greater act of obedience. His intent is that the doer of disobedience either: he had previously performed an act of obedience whose reward was greater than the punishment of this disobedience, or the matter is not so. If the first, this disobedience is minor and its punishment is nullified; if the second, this disobedience is major and its punishment is not removed except by repentance. The position of our companions is that God, Exalted, may pardon a major sin after repentance, and this verse indicates that, and its explanation is from several aspects:

First: forgiveness of a major sin after repentance and forgiveness of a minor sin are among the matters obligatory upon the servant, and all the prophets and saints and righteous among ordinary people share in performing obligations. So if we take His being "Forgiver of sin" in this sense, there would remain no difference between Him and the least of the company of the obedient in the meaning that warrants this praise, and that is false. Thus it is established that it must mean His being Forgiver of major sins before repentance, which is what is sought.

Second: forgiveness is an expression for covering, and the meaning of covering is conceivable only in a thing that remains existing so that it may be covered, whereas a minor sin is nullified by the abundance of the reward of its doer, so the meaning of forgiving in it is not conceivable. It is also not possible to take His saying "Forgiver of sin" to mean major sin after repentance, because the meaning of His being "Acceptor of repentance" is nothing but that, so if the intent of His being "Forgiver of sin" were this meaning, it would entail repetition, which is false. Thus it is established that His being "Forgiver of sin" indicates His being Forgiver of major sins before repentance.

Third: His saying "Forgiver of sin" is mentioned in the context of great praise, so it must be taken to indicate the greatest kind of praise, and that is His being Forgiver of major sins before repentance, which is what is sought.

Page 25

The second attribute: His saying, Exalted is He, "Acceptor of repentance." On this there are two discussions.

First: concerning the word tawb (repentance) there are two views. The first: it is a verbal noun, this is the view of Abu 'Ubayda. The second: it is the plural of tawbah (repentance), this is the view of al-Akhfash. Al-Mubarrad said: it may be a verbal noun, one says: taba yatubu tawban and tawbatan, like qala yaqulu qawlan and qawlatan; and it may be a plural of tawbah, so it would be tawbah and tawb, like tamrah and tamr; but the verbal noun is closer, because on this reckoning its interpretation is that He accepts this action.

Second: the position of our companions is that the acceptance of repentance from the sinner occurs by way of grace (tafaddul), and is not obligatory upon God. The Mu'tazilites said: it is obligatory upon God. Our companions argued that He, Exalted, mentioned His being Acceptor of repentance as a matter of praise and commendation, and if that were obligatory, little of the meaning of praise would remain in it, only the small measure that is obtained by all the righteous when performing obligations and abstaining from prohibitions.

* * *

The third attribute: His saying "Severe in punishment." On this there are discussions:

First discussion: there is an objection to this verse, which is that His saying "Severe in punishment" may be an adjective of an indefinite noun but may not be an adjective of a definite noun. You say: "I passed by a man severe in strength," but you do not say: "I passed by 'Abd Allah severe in strength." And His saying "Allah" is a proper name, so it is definite, so how is it permissible to describe Him as severe in punishment when it can only be made an adjective of an indefinite noun? They said: this is unlike our saying "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance," because what is meant by them is not the occurrence of these two actions now or tomorrow, but that the affirmation and permanence of this is intended, so their ruling is the ruling of "God of creation" and "Lord of the Throne." As for "Severe in punishment," it is problematic, because it is in the sense of "severe is His punishment," so it would be indefinite, and thus it is not valid to make it an adjective of a definite noun. This is the statement of the objection. It was answered in several ways:

First: although this attribute is indefinite, when it is mentioned together with the other attributes which are definite, its mention is acceptable, as in His saying: "And He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Lord of the Glorious Throne, Accomplisher of what He wills" [al-Buruj: 14–16].

Second: al-Zajjaj said: the genitive of "Severe in punishment" is in apposition (badal), because making an indefinite noun an apposition of a definite noun and the reverse is permissible. They objected to this, saying that making it alone an apposition of the attributes contains evident weakness.

Third: there is no dispute that His saying "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance" may be made attributes, and it is so because they convey the meaning of permanence and continuity; likewise His saying "Severe in punishment" conveys the meaning of permanence and continuity, because the attributes of God, Exalted, are free from occurrence and renewal, so His being severe in punishment means His being such that His punishment is severe, and this meaning is always present, and it is not described as having come about after not being so. This is what has been said on this topic.

Second discussion: this verse suggests the preference of the side of mercy and grace, because when He, Exalted, wished to describe Himself as severe in punishment, He mentioned before it two matters, each of which requires the removal of punishment, namely His being Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance, and He mentioned after it what indicates the attainment of great mercy, namely His saying "Possessor of bounty." So His being severe in punishment, since it was preceded by those two attributes and followed by this attribute, indicates that the side of mercy and generosity is weightier.

Third discussion: one may ask: He mentioned the conjunction "wa" (and) in His saying "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance," but did not mention it in His saying "Severe in punishment." What is the difference? We say: if He had not mentioned the "wa" in His saying "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance," it would be possible that it might occur to a person that there is no meaning to His being Forgiver of sin except His being Acceptor of repentance. But since He mentioned the "wa," this possibility is removed, because conjoining a thing with itself is impossible. As for His being severe in punishment, it is known that it is distinct from His being "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance," so He dispensed with mentioning the "wa" for it.

The fourth attribute: "Possessor of bounty" (dhī al-ṭawl), meaning dhī al-tafaddul (the Possessor of favour). It is said: ṭāla ʿalaynā ṭawlan, i.e., he showed favour to us with favour. And from their speech: ṭul ʿalayya bi-faḍlika (show me favour by Your grace). And from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those of means among them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 86], and its tafsir has passed at His saying: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford [ṭawlan] to marry free believing women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25].

Know that when He described Himself as ﴿severe in punishment﴾, it must be that the meaning of His being one who brings severe punishment is that it is not ugly for Him to bring it, indeed it is not permissible to describe Him as one who commits an ugly act. Given this is established, we say: He mentioned after it His being dhū al-ṭawl, which is His being dhū al-faḍl (Possessor of grace). Therefore its meaning must be His being Possessor of grace by virtue of refraining from the punishment which He has the right to inflict; for He mentioned His being dhū al-ṭawl without specifying in what respect He is dhū al-ṭawl, so it is obligatory to restrict it to His being dhū al-ṭawl in the matter previously mentioned, which is the infliction of the punishment that is good, to avoid ambiguity. This indicates that He may refrain from the punishment which it would have been good for Him to inflict, and this indicates that pardoning the people of major sins is permissible, which is what was sought.

The fifth attribute: absolute monotheism (al-tawḥīd al-muṭlaq), which is His saying: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. The meaning is that He described Himself with attributes of mercy and grace; so if there were with Him another god who shared with Him and equalled Him in the attribute of mercy and grace, the need to worship Him would not be intense. But when He is One, having no partner nor likeness, the need to acknowledge His worship is intense, and so complete encouragement and warning are attained through this tawḥīd.

The sixth attribute: His saying: ﴿To Him is the final return﴾. This attribute also strengthens the desire to acknowledge His worship; for even assuming He is described with attributes of grace and generosity and is One without partner, yet if the doctrine of resurrection and gathering were false, the intense fear from disobeying Him would not arise. But since the doctrine of the gathering and the Resurrection is established, the fear is greater and the caution more complete. For this reason God, exalted is He, mentioned these attributes. The anthropomorphists (ahl al-tashbīh) argued from the particle (ilā, "to"), saying that it indicates the end of a limit. The answer to this is mentioned in many places in this book.

* * *

Know that when He, exalted is He, established that the Qur'an is a Book which He sent down to be guided by in the religion, He mentioned the states of those who dispute in order to nullify it and conceal its matter, saying: ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾. In this there are issues:

The first issue: disputation is of two kinds: disputation in establishing the truth and disputation in establishing falsehood. As for disputation in establishing the truth, it is the craft of the prophets, peace be upon them. God, exalted is He, said to Muhammad ﷺ: ﴿And argue with them in the best manner﴾ [al-Naḥl: 125], and He related of the disbelievers that they said to Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿O Noah, you have disputed with us and have much disputed with us﴾ [Hud: 32].

Page 27

As for disputation in establishing falsehood, it is blameworthy, and it is what is meant by this verse where He says: ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾. And He said: ﴿They did not present it to you except as a dispute; rather they are a contentious people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58], and He said: ﴿And they disputed with falsehood to refute thereby the truth﴾. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, disputing about the Qur'an is kufr." So His saying "indeed, a dispute (jidāl) in the Qur'an" in indefinite form indicates a distinction between one dispute and another. Know that the expression "jidāl fī al-shay'" (dispute about a thing) implies disputing falsehood, while "jidāl ʿan al-shay'" (dispute on behalf of a thing) implies disputing for the sake of establishing it and defending it. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, disputing in the Qur'an is kufr," and he said: "Do not dispute about the Qur'an, for wrangling over it is kufr."

The second issue: disputing concerning the signs of God is to say at one time that it is magic, at another that it is poetry, at another that it is the speech of soothsayers, at another the fables of the ancients, and at another that a human is teaching it, and similar baseless doubts that they used to voice. God mentioned that none does this except those who disbelieve and turn away from the truth.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So let not their movement throughout the lands deceive you﴾, meaning: you should not be deceived into thinking that I am giving them respite and leaving them safe in their bodies and wealth, moving about in the lands, i.e., engaging in trade and seeking livelihood. For although I give them respite, I will seize them and take vengeance upon them, as I did to their like among the earlier nations. Quraysh were likewise moving about in the lands of Syria and Yemen, and had great wealth with which they traded and profited. Then He revealed this meaning, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and the factions after them﴾. So He mentioned among those deniers the people of Noah, ﴿and the factions after them﴾, i.e., the nations persisting in disbelief, such as the people of ʿĀd, Thamūd and others, as He said in Surah Ṣād: ﴿The people of Noah and ʿĀd and Pharaoh of the stakes denied before them, and Thamūd and the people of Lot and the companions of the thicket; those are the factions﴾ [Ṣād: 12–13]. And His saying: ﴿And every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him﴾, i.e., each nation of these factions resolved to seize their messenger in order to kill him, torture him, or imprison him. ﴿And they disputed with falsehood﴾, i.e., these people disputed with their messengers by falsehood, namely by raising doubts; ﴿to refute thereby the truth﴾, i.e., to remove by means of those doubts the truth and sincerity. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾, i.e., I brought upon them the destruction which they had intended to bring upon the messengers, and they had wished to seize them, but I seized them, so how was My punishment of them? Was it not destroying, uprooting, and awe-inspiring in mention and in hearing? So I will do to your people as I did to these, if they persist in disbelief and dispute concerning the signs of God. Then He revealed this meaning, saying: ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has been fulfilled against those who disbelieve, that they are the companions of the Fire﴾, i.e., just as the punishment was decreed upon those earlier nations, so My word is likewise fulfilled against those of your people who disbelieved; so they are on the verge of the descent of punishment upon them. The author of al-Kashshāf said: ﴿that they are the companions of the Fire﴾ is in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for "the word of your Lord", i.e., the same obligation became binding upon the disbelievers that they are of the companions of the Fire; its meaning: just as their destruction in this world by an uprooting punishment became obligatory, so too their destruction by the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter became obligatory. Or it is in the accusative position, with the particle of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) removed and the verb made to reach its object.

Our companions argued from this verse that God's decree of happiness and wretchedness is binding and cannot be changed. They said: He, exalted is He, informed that the word of punishment has been fulfilled against them, and this indicates that they have no capacity to believe; for if they were able to do so, they would be able to nullify this true word, and they would be able to nullify the knowledge and wisdom of God, since it is necessary that whoever is able to do something must be able to do everything that is among its necessary consequences. Moreover, if they believed, it would have been obligatory upon them to believe in this verse, and then they would have believed that they will never believe, and that is the imposition of what cannot be borne. Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read "ḥaqqat kalimātu rabbika" in the plural, and the rest read it in the singular.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So let not their movement throughout the lands deceive you﴾, meaning: you should not be deceived into thinking that I am giving them respite and leaving them safe in their bodies and wealth, moving about in the lands, i.e., engaging in trade and seeking livelihood. For although I give them respite, I will seize them and take vengeance upon them, as I did to their like among the earlier nations. Quraysh were likewise moving about in the lands of Syria and Yemen, and had great wealth with which they traded and profited. Then He revealed this meaning, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and the factions after them﴾. Our companions argued from this verse that God's decree of happiness and wretchedness is binding and cannot be changed. They said: He, exalted is He, informed that the word of punishment has been fulfilled against them, and this indicates that they have no capacity to believe; for if they were able to do so, they would be able to nullify this true word, and they would be able to nullify the knowledge and wisdom of God, since it is necessary that whoever is able to do something must be able to do everything that is among its necessary consequences. Know that there are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, and Hamza and al-Kisa'i, read "Ha" (ḥāʾ) with a kasra (ḥā), while the rest read it with a fatha (ḥa). Nafi' in some transmissions and Ibn 'Amir read it between fatha and kasra, meaning that they do not pronounce it with a full fatha. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: it was read with fatha and with sukun on the mim. The reason for fatha is movement to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn) and preference for the lightest vowels, like ayna and kayfa; or it is in the accusative by implying "read" (iqra'). Its non-declension (man' al-sarf) is either due to feminine gender and definiteness, since it is a name of the surah and is definite, and because it is of the pattern of a foreign name like Qabil and Habil. As for sukun, it is because we have explained that names are mentioned in their pausal form.

The second issue: The exhaustive discussion of these opening letters is mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. The closer view here is that one says: "Ha Mim" is the name of the surah. So His saying "Ha Mim" is a subject (mubtada'), and His saying "The revelation of the Book from God" is the predicate (khabar). The implied meaning is that this surah called Ha Mim is the revelation of the Book. So "tanzil" is a verbal noun (masdar), but what is meant by it is the thing revealed (munazzal).

As for His saying "from God": know that when He mentioned that "Ha Mim, the revelation of the Book," it became necessary to explain who the One who revealed it is. So He said "from God." Then He explained that God, Exalted, is described with attributes of majesty and marks of greatness, so that this would move one to exert full effort when listening and would restrain one from negligence and slackness in it. So He explained that the Revealer is "God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing."

Know that people differ concerning what knowledge of God is. A great group said: it is knowledge that He is capable, and after that knowledge that He is knowing. Once you know this, we say: "al-'Aziz" has two interpretations. The first: the Overpowering, so its meaning is the Capable whom no one equals in power. The second: the One who has no like. It is not permissible that "al-'Aziz" here means the Capable, because His saying "Allah" already indicates His being capable, so "al-'Aziz" must be understood in the second sense, which is the One who has no like. And whatever is like this must not be a body, and whatever is not a body is free from appetite and aversion, and whatever is like that is free from need. As for "al-'Alim," it is an intensive form for knowledge, and complete intensiveness is realized only when He, Exalted, knows all things known. So His saying "from God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing" returns in meaning to: this Book is a revelation from the Absolutely Capable, the Absolutely Self-Sufficient, the Absolutely Knowing. Whoever is like this knows the aspects of benefit and harm, and knows that He is independent of attracting benefits and repelling harms. Whoever is like this is merciful and generous, and His actions are wisdom and rightness, free from ugliness and falsehood. So it is as if He, glorified is He, mentioned these three names after His saying "revelation" only because they indicate that His actions are wisdom and rightness, and when this is so, it follows that this revelation is truth and rightness.

The second: He undertook its preservation, the generality of the obligation in it, and its manifestation until the end of obligation, and this is not complete except by His being Mighty, who is not overcome, and by His being All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden. The first attribute: His saying "the Forgiver of sin." Al-Jubba'i said: its meaning is that He is the Forgiver of sin when He deserves forgiveness, either through repentance or through a greater act of obedience. His intent is that the doer of disobedience either: he had previously performed an act of obedience whose reward was greater than the punishment of this disobedience, or the matter is not so. If the first, this disobedience is minor and its punishment is nullified; if the second, this disobedience is major and its punishment is not removed except by repentance. The position of our companions is that God, Exalted, may pardon a major sin after repentance, and this verse indicates that, and its explanation is from several aspects:

So if we take His being "Forgiver of sin" in this sense, there would remain no difference between Him and the least of the company of the obedient in the meaning that warrants this praise, and that is false. Thus it is established that it must mean His being Forgiver of major sins before repentance, which is what is sought.

Second: forgiveness is an expression for covering, and the meaning of covering is conceivable only in a thing that remains existing so that it may be covered, whereas a minor sin is nullified by the abundance of the reward of its doer, so the meaning of forgiving in it is not conceivable. It is also not possible to take His saying "Forgiver of sin" to mean major sin after repentance, because the meaning of His being "Acceptor of repentance" is nothing but that, so if the intent of His being "Forgiver of sin" were this meaning, it would entail repetition, which is false. Thus it is established that His being "Forgiver of sin" indicates His being Forgiver of major sins before repentance.

Third: His saying "Forgiver of sin" is mentioned in the context of great praise, so it must be taken to indicate the greatest kind of praise, and that is His being Forgiver of major sins before repentance, which is what is sought.

The reason for fatha is movement to avoid the meeting of two unvocalized letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn) and preference for the lightest vowels, like ayna and kayfa; or it is in the accusative by implying "read" (iqra'). Its non-declension (man' al-sarf) is either due to feminine gender and definiteness, since it is a name of the surah and is definite, and because it is of the pattern of a foreign name like Qabil and Habil. As for sukun, it is because we have explained that names are mentioned in their pausal form.

The second issue: The exhaustive discussion of these opening letters is mentioned at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. The closer view here is that one says: "Ha Mim" is the name of the surah. So His saying "Ha Mim" is a subject (mubtada'), and His saying "The revelation of the Book from God" is the predicate (khabar). The implied meaning is that this surah called Ha Mim is the revelation of the Book. So "tanzil" is a verbal noun (masdar), but what is meant by it is the thing revealed (munazzal).

* * *

As for His saying "from God": know that when He mentioned that "Ha Mim, the revelation of the Book," it became necessary to explain who the One who revealed it is. So He said "from God." Then He explained that God, Exalted, is described with attributes of majesty and marks of greatness, so that this would move one to exert full effort when listening and would restrain one from negligence and slackness in it. So He explained that the Revealer is "God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing."

Know that people differ concerning what knowledge of God is. A great group said: it is knowledge that He is capable, and after that knowledge that He is knowing. Once you know this, we say: "al-'Aziz" has two interpretations. The first: the Overpowering, so its meaning is the Capable whom no one equals in power. The second: the One who has no like. It is not permissible that "al-'Aziz" here means the Capable, because His saying "Allah" already indicates His being capable, so "al-'Aziz" must be understood in the second sense, which is the One who has no like. And whatever is like this must not be a body, and whatever is not a body is free from appetite and aversion, and whatever is like that is free from need. As for "al-'Alim," it is an intensive form for knowledge, and complete intensiveness is realized only when He, Exalted, knows all things known. So His saying "from God, the Mighty, the All-Knowing" returns in meaning to: this Book is a revelation from the Absolutely Capable, the Absolutely Self-Sufficient, the Absolutely Knowing. Whoever is like this knows the aspects of benefit and harm, and knows that He is independent of attracting benefits and repelling harms. Whoever is like this is merciful and generous, and His actions are wisdom and rightness, free from ugliness and falsehood. So it is as if He, glorified is He, mentioned these three names after His saying "revelation" only because they indicate that His actions are wisdom and rightness, and when this is so, it follows that this revelation is truth and rightness.

It has also been said: the benefit in mentioning "al-'Aziz al-'Alim" is twofold. The first: by His power and knowledge He sent down the Qur'an in this measure which contains benefits and inimitability, and were He not Mighty and All-Knowing, this would not be valid. The second: He undertook its preservation, the generality of the obligation in it, and its manifestation until the end of obligation, and this is not complete except by His being Mighty, who is not overcome, and by His being All-Knowing, from whom nothing is hidden. Then He described Himself with what combines promise and threat, fear and hope, saying: "the Forgiver of sin, the Acceptor of repentance, Severe in punishment, Possessor of bounty. There is no god but Him; to Him is the final return." These are six kinds of attributes:

The first attribute: His saying "the Forgiver of sin." Al-Jubba'i said: its meaning is that He is the Forgiver of sin when He deserves forgiveness, either through repentance or through a greater act of obedience. His intent is that the doer of disobedience either: he had previously performed an act of obedience whose reward was greater than the punishment of this disobedience, or the matter is not so. If the first, this disobedience is minor and its punishment is nullified; if the second, this disobedience is major and its punishment is not removed except by repentance. The position of our companions is that God, Exalted, may pardon a major sin after repentance, and this verse indicates that, and its explanation is from several aspects:

First: forgiveness of a major sin after repentance and forgiveness of a minor sin are among the matters obligatory upon the servant, and all the prophets and saints and righteous among ordinary people share in performing obligations. So if we take His being "Forgiver of sin" in this sense, there would remain no difference between Him and the least of the company of the obedient in the meaning that warrants this praise, and that is false. Thus it is established that it must mean His being Forgiver of major sins before repentance, which is what is sought.

Second: forgiveness is an expression for covering, and the meaning of covering is conceivable only in a thing that remains existing so that it may be covered, whereas a minor sin is nullified by the abundance of the reward of its doer, so the meaning of forgiving in it is not conceivable. It is also not possible to take His saying "Forgiver of sin" to mean major sin after repentance, because the meaning of His being "Acceptor of repentance" is nothing but that, so if the intent of His being "Forgiver of sin" were this meaning, it would entail repetition, which is false. Thus it is established that His being "Forgiver of sin" indicates His being Forgiver of major sins before repentance.

Third: His saying "Forgiver of sin" is mentioned in the context of great praise, so it must be taken to indicate the greatest kind of praise, and that is His being Forgiver of major sins before repentance, which is what is sought.

Page 25

The second attribute: His saying, Exalted is He, "Acceptor of repentance." On this there are two discussions.

First: concerning the word tawb (repentance) there are two views. The first: it is a verbal noun, this is the view of Abu 'Ubayda. The second: it is the plural of tawbah (repentance), this is the view of al-Akhfash. Al-Mubarrad said: it may be a verbal noun, one says: taba yatubu tawban and tawbatan, like qala yaqulu qawlan and qawlatan; and it may be a plural of tawbah, so it would be tawbah and tawb, like tamrah and tamr; but the verbal noun is closer, because on this reckoning its interpretation is that He accepts this action.

Second: the position of our companions is that the acceptance of repentance from the sinner occurs by way of grace (tafaddul), and is not obligatory upon God. The Mu'tazilites said: it is obligatory upon God. Our companions argued that He, Exalted, mentioned His being Acceptor of repentance as a matter of praise and commendation, and if that were obligatory, little of the meaning of praise would remain in it, only the small measure that is obtained by all the righteous when performing obligations and abstaining from prohibitions.

* * *

The third attribute: His saying "Severe in punishment." On this there are discussions:

First discussion: there is an objection to this verse, which is that His saying "Severe in punishment" may be an adjective of an indefinite noun but may not be an adjective of a definite noun. You say: "I passed by a man severe in strength," but you do not say: "I passed by 'Abd Allah severe in strength." And His saying "Allah" is a proper name, so it is definite, so how is it permissible to describe Him as severe in punishment when it can only be made an adjective of an indefinite noun? They said: this is unlike our saying "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance," because what is meant by them is not the occurrence of these two actions now or tomorrow, but that the affirmation and permanence of this is intended, so their ruling is the ruling of "God of creation" and "Lord of the Throne." As for "Severe in punishment," it is problematic, because it is in the sense of "severe is His punishment," so it would be indefinite, and thus it is not valid to make it an adjective of a definite noun. This is the statement of the objection. It was answered in several ways:

First: although this attribute is indefinite, when it is mentioned together with the other attributes which are definite, its mention is acceptable, as in His saying: "And He is the Forgiving, the Loving, Lord of the Glorious Throne, Accomplisher of what He wills" [al-Buruj: 14–16].

Second: al-Zajjaj said: the genitive of "Severe in punishment" is in apposition (badal), because making an indefinite noun an apposition of a definite noun and the reverse is permissible. They objected to this, saying that making it alone an apposition of the attributes contains evident weakness.

Third: there is no dispute that His saying "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance" may be made attributes, and it is so because they convey the meaning of permanence and continuity; likewise His saying "Severe in punishment" conveys the meaning of permanence and continuity, because the attributes of God, Exalted, are free from occurrence and renewal, so His being severe in punishment means His being such that His punishment is severe, and this meaning is always present, and it is not described as having come about after not being so. This is what has been said on this topic.

Second discussion: this verse suggests the preference of the side of mercy and grace, because when He, Exalted, wished to describe Himself as severe in punishment, He mentioned before it two matters, each of which requires the removal of punishment, namely His being Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance, and He mentioned after it what indicates the attainment of great mercy, namely His saying "Possessor of bounty." So His being severe in punishment, since it was preceded by those two attributes and followed by this attribute, indicates that the side of mercy and generosity is weightier.

Third discussion: one may ask: He mentioned the conjunction "wa" (and) in His saying "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance," but did not mention it in His saying "Severe in punishment." What is the difference? We say: if He had not mentioned the "wa" in His saying "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance," it would be possible that it might occur to a person that there is no meaning to His being Forgiver of sin except His being Acceptor of repentance. But since He mentioned the "wa," this possibility is removed, because conjoining a thing with itself is impossible. As for His being severe in punishment, it is known that it is distinct from His being "Forgiver of sin and Acceptor of repentance," so He dispensed with mentioning the "wa" for it.

The fourth attribute: "Possessor of bounty" (dhī al-ṭawl), meaning dhī al-tafaddul (the Possessor of favour). It is said: ṭāla ʿalaynā ṭawlan, i.e., he showed favour to us with favour. And from their speech: ṭul ʿalayya bi-faḍlika (show me favour by Your grace). And from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those of means among them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 86], and its tafsir has passed at His saying: ﴿And whoever among you cannot afford [ṭawlan] to marry free believing women﴾ [al-Nisa': 25].

Know that when He described Himself as ﴿severe in punishment﴾, it must be that the meaning of His being one who brings severe punishment is that it is not ugly for Him to bring it, indeed it is not permissible to describe Him as one who commits an ugly act. Given this is established, we say: He mentioned after it His being dhū al-ṭawl, which is His being dhū al-faḍl (Possessor of grace). Therefore its meaning must be His being Possessor of grace by virtue of refraining from the punishment which He has the right to inflict; for He mentioned His being dhū al-ṭawl without specifying in what respect He is dhū al-ṭawl, so it is obligatory to restrict it to His being dhū al-ṭawl in the matter previously mentioned, which is the infliction of the punishment that is good, to avoid ambiguity. This indicates that He may refrain from the punishment which it would have been good for Him to inflict, and this indicates that pardoning the people of major sins is permissible, which is what was sought.

The fifth attribute: absolute monotheism (al-tawḥīd al-muṭlaq), which is His saying: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. The meaning is that He described Himself with attributes of mercy and grace; so if there were with Him another god who shared with Him and equalled Him in the attribute of mercy and grace, the need to worship Him would not be intense. But when He is One, having no partner nor likeness, the need to acknowledge His worship is intense, and so complete encouragement and warning are attained through this tawḥīd.

The sixth attribute: His saying: ﴿To Him is the final return﴾. This attribute also strengthens the desire to acknowledge His worship; for even assuming He is described with attributes of grace and generosity and is One without partner, yet if the doctrine of resurrection and gathering were false, the intense fear from disobeying Him would not arise. But since the doctrine of the gathering and the Resurrection is established, the fear is greater and the caution more complete. For this reason God, exalted is He, mentioned these attributes. The anthropomorphists (ahl al-tashbīh) argued from the particle (ilā, "to"), saying that it indicates the end of a limit. The answer to this is mentioned in many places in this book.

As for disputation in establishing falsehood, it is blameworthy, and it is what is meant by this verse where He says: ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾. As for disputation in establishing falsehood, it is blameworthy, and it is what is meant by this verse where He says: ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of God except those who disbelieve﴾. And He said: ﴿They did not present it to you except as a dispute; rather they are a contentious people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58], and He said: ﴿And they disputed with falsehood to refute thereby the truth﴾. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, disputing about the Qur'an is kufr." So His saying "indeed, a dispute (jidāl) in the Qur'an" in indefinite form indicates a distinction between one dispute and another. Know that the expression "jidāl fī al-shay'" (dispute about a thing) implies disputing falsehood, while "jidāl ʿan al-shay'" (dispute on behalf of a thing) implies disputing for the sake of establishing it and defending it. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, disputing in the Qur'an is kufr," and he said: "Do not dispute about the Qur'an, for wrangling over it is kufr."

The second issue: disputing concerning the signs of God is to say at one time that it is magic, at another that it is poetry, at another that it is the speech of soothsayers, at another the fables of the ancients, and at another that a human is teaching it, and similar baseless doubts that they used to voice. God mentioned that none does this except those who disbelieve and turn away from the truth.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So let not their movement throughout the lands deceive you﴾, meaning: you should not be deceived into thinking that I am giving them respite and leaving them safe in their bodies and wealth, moving about in the lands, i.e., engaging in trade and seeking livelihood. For although I give them respite, I will seize them and take vengeance upon them, as I did to their like among the earlier nations. Quraysh were likewise moving about in the lands of Syria and Yemen, and had great wealth with which they traded and profited. Then He revealed this meaning, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and the factions after them﴾. So He mentioned among those deniers the people of Noah, ﴿and the factions after them﴾, i.e., the nations persisting in disbelief, such as the people of ʿĀd, Thamūd and others, as He said in Surah Ṣād: ﴿The people of Noah and ʿĀd and Pharaoh of the stakes denied before them, and Thamūd and the people of Lot and the companions of the thicket; those are the factions﴾ [Ṣād: 12–13]. Was it not destroying, uprooting, and awe-inspiring in mention and in hearing? So I will do to your people as I did to these, if they persist in disbelief and dispute concerning the signs of God. Then He revealed this meaning, saying: ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has been fulfilled against those who disbelieve, that they are the companions of the Fire﴾, i.e., just as the punishment was decreed upon those earlier nations, so My word is likewise fulfilled against those of your people who disbelieved; so they are on the verge of the descent of punishment upon them. The author of al-Kashshāf said: ﴿that they are the companions of the Fire﴾ is in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for "the word of your Lord", i.e., the same obligation became binding upon the disbelievers that they are of the companions of the Fire; its meaning: just as their destruction in this world by an uprooting punishment became obligatory, so too their destruction by the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter became obligatory. Or it is in the accusative position, with the particle of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) removed and the verb made to reach its object.

Our companions argued from this verse that God's decree of happiness and wretchedness is binding and cannot be changed. They said: He, exalted is He, informed that the word of punishment has been fulfilled against them, and this indicates that they have no capacity to believe; for if they were able to do so, they would be able to nullify this true word, and they would be able to nullify the knowledge and wisdom of God, since it is necessary that whoever is able to do something must be able to do everything that is among its necessary consequences. Moreover, if they believed, it would have been obligatory upon them to believe in this verse, and then they would have believed that they will never believe, and that is the imposition of what cannot be borne. Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read "ḥaqqat kalimātu rabbika" in the plural, and the rest read it in the singular.

And He said: ﴿They did not present it to you except as a dispute; rather they are a contentious people﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 58], and He said: ﴿And they disputed with falsehood to refute thereby the truth﴾. And the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, disputing about the Qur'an is kufr." So His saying "indeed, a dispute (jidāl) in the Qur'an" in indefinite form indicates a distinction between one dispute and another. Know that the expression "jidāl fī al-shay'" (dispute about a thing) implies disputing falsehood, while "jidāl ʿan al-shay'" (dispute on behalf of a thing) implies disputing for the sake of establishing it and defending it. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, disputing in the Qur'an is kufr," and he said: "Do not dispute about the Qur'an, for wrangling over it is kufr."

The second issue: disputing concerning the signs of God is to say at one time that it is magic, at another that it is poetry, at another that it is the speech of soothsayers, at another the fables of the ancients, and at another that a human is teaching it, and similar baseless doubts that they used to voice. God mentioned that none does this except those who disbelieve and turn away from the truth.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿So let not their movement throughout the lands deceive you﴾, meaning: you should not be deceived into thinking that I am giving them respite and leaving them safe in their bodies and wealth, moving about in the lands, i.e., engaging in trade and seeking livelihood. For although I give them respite, I will seize them and take vengeance upon them, as I did to their like among the earlier nations. Quraysh were likewise moving about in the lands of Syria and Yemen, and had great wealth with which they traded and profited. Then He revealed this meaning, saying: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, and the factions after them﴾. So He mentioned among those deniers the people of Noah, ﴿and the factions after them﴾, i.e., the nations persisting in disbelief, such as the people of ʿĀd, Thamūd and others, as He said in Surah Ṣād: ﴿The people of Noah and ʿĀd and Pharaoh of the stakes denied before them, and Thamūd and the people of Lot and the companions of the thicket; those are the factions﴾ [Ṣād: 12–13]. And His saying: ﴿And every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him﴾, i.e., each nation of these factions resolved to seize their messenger in order to kill him, torture him, or imprison him. ﴿And they disputed with falsehood﴾, i.e., these people disputed with their messengers by falsehood, namely by raising doubts; ﴿to refute thereby the truth﴾, i.e., to remove by means of those doubts the truth and sincerity. ﴿Then I seized them, so how was My punishment?﴾, i.e., I brought upon them the destruction which they had intended to bring upon the messengers, and they had wished to seize them, but I seized them, so how was My punishment of them? Was it not destroying, uprooting, and awe-inspiring in mention and in hearing? So I will do to your people as I did to these, if they persist in disbelief and dispute concerning the signs of God. Then He revealed this meaning, saying: ﴿Thus the word of your Lord has been fulfilled against those who disbelieve, that they are the companions of the Fire﴾, i.e., just as the punishment was decreed upon those earlier nations, so My word is likewise fulfilled against those of your people who disbelieved; so they are on the verge of the descent of punishment upon them. The author of al-Kashshāf said: ﴿that they are the companions of the Fire﴾ is in the nominative position as a substitute (badal) for "the word of your Lord", i.e., the same obligation became binding upon the disbelievers that they are of the companions of the Fire; its meaning: just as their destruction in this world by an uprooting punishment became obligatory, so too their destruction by the punishment of the Fire in the Hereafter became obligatory. Or it is in the accusative position, with the particle of causation (lām al-taʿlīl) removed and the verb made to reach its object.

Our companions argued from this verse that God's decree of happiness and wretchedness is binding and cannot be changed. They said: He, exalted is He, informed that the word of punishment has been fulfilled against them, and this indicates that they have no capacity to believe; for if they were able to do so, they would be able to nullify this true word, and they would be able to nullify the knowledge and wisdom of God, since it is necessary that whoever is able to do something must be able to do everything that is among its necessary consequences. Moreover, if they believed, it would have been obligatory upon them to believe in this verse, and then they would have believed that they will never believe, and that is the imposition of what cannot be borne. Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir read "ḥaqqat kalimātu rabbika" in the plural, and the rest read it in the singular.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 40, verse 7–9 (part 1 of 3):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise, and believe in Him, and ask forgiveness for those who believe: "Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and protect them from the punishment of the Blazing Fire."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, and admit them into the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them, along with whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their descendants. Indeed, You are the Mighty, the Wise."﴾ ﴿"And protect them from evil deeds. Whoever You protect from evil deeds on that Day, You have indeed shown them mercy. That is the great triumph."﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that the disbelievers exaggerate in displaying enmity towards the believers, He explained that the noblest of the classes of created beings are the angels who are the bearers of the Throne, and those who surround the Throne, who exaggerate in displaying love and support for the believers. It is as if He, exalted is He, says: If these lowly ones exaggerate in enmity, then do not care for them, do not turn to them, and do not give them any weight, for the bearers of the Throne are with you, and those around the Throne are with you, supporting you. There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: He, exalted is He, related this account concerning two kinds of groups of angels:

The first category: ﴿those who bear the Throne﴾. Exalted is He has related that those who bear the Throne on the Day of Resurrection are eight. It may be said: those who bear it at this time are those same eight who will bear it on the Day of Resurrection. And there is no doubt that the bearers of the Throne are the noblest and greatest of the angels. Ṣāḥib al-Kashshāf (al-Zamakhshari) related that the feet of the bearers of the Throne are in the lowest earth and their heads have pierced the Throne, and they are in humble submission, not raising their gaze. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Do not reflect upon the greatness of your Lord, but reflect upon what Allah, exalted is He, has created of the angels, for indeed there is a created angel called Israfil, whose corner of the Throne is upon his shoulder, and his feet are in the lowest earth, and his head has passed through seven heavens, and he shrinks from the greatness of Allah until he becomes like a small thing." It was said: he is a small bird. It has also been narrated that Allah commanded all the angels to greet the bearers of the Throne with peace morning and evening, as a preference for them over the rest of the angels. It was also said: Allah created the Throne from a green jewel, and between two of its legs the flapping of a swiftly flying bird lasts eighty thousand years. It was also said: around the Throne are seventy thousand rows of angels circling it, glorifying and magnifying, and behind them are seventy thousand rows standing with their hands placed upon their shoulders, raising their voices in tahlil and takbir, and behind them are a hundred thousand rows with their right hands placed upon their left. There is not one of them but glorifies with something other than what the other glorifies. I have transmitted these reports from al-Kashshaf.

As for the second category of angels mentioned by Allah in this verse, it is His saying: ﴿and those around it﴾. The more apparent meaning is that what is meant by them is what He mentioned in His saying: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying their Lord with praise.﴾

I say: Reason indicates that the bearers of the Throne and those surrounding the Throne must be the best of the angels. That is because the relation of spirits to spirits is like the relation of bodies to bodies. So when the Throne was the noblest of corporeal existents, the spirits attached to governing the Throne must be better than the spirits governing bodies. Also, it is likely that there are spirits bearing the body of the Throne, and from those dominant, elevated spirits bearing the body of the Throne there come forth other spirits of their kind, attached to the edges of the Throne, and to them refers His saying: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne.﴾ In sum, it has become clear by certain proofs and by true unveilings that there is no comparison between the world of bodies and the world of spirits. So whatever you witness with the eye of sight in the varying ranks of the world of bodies, you must witness with the eye of insight in the varying ranks of the world of spirits.

The second issue: This verse indicates that He, glorified is He, is far above being in the Throne. That is because He, exalted is He, said in this verse: ﴿those who bear the Throne﴾, and He said in another verse: ﴿And above them on that Day eight will bear the Throne of your Lord﴾ [al-Haqqah: 17]. There is no doubt that the bearer of the Throne is a bearer of everything in the Throne. So if the God of the world were in the Throne, these angels would be bearing the God of the world, and then they would be guarding the God of the world. The guardian, being capable, is more deserving of divinity, and the one borne and guarded is more deserving of servitude. Then the god would become a servant and the servant a god, and that is corrupt. This shows that the God of the Throne and of bodies is exalted above the Throne and bodies.

* * *

Know that He, exalted is He, related three things concerning the bearers of the Throne and those surrounding the Throne:

The first type is His saying: ﴿they glorify their Lord with praise﴾. Its parallel is His saying, relating about the angels: ﴿while we glorify You with Your praise﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30], and His saying: ﴿And you will see the angels surrounding the Throne, glorifying their Lord with praise.﴾ Thus tasbih is an expression for declaring Allah far above what is unfitting, and tahmid is acknowledging that He is the absolute Bestower of blessings. So tasbih points to majesty (jalal) and tahmid points to generosity (ikram). Thus His saying ﴿they glorify their Lord with praise﴾ is close to His saying: ﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord, Possessor of Majesty and Honour﴾ [al-Rahman: 78].

The second type of what Allah related about these angels is His saying: ﴿and they believe in Him.﴾ If it is asked: what is the benefit of His saying ﴿and they believe in Him﴾, since occupation with glorification and praise is not possible unless faith in Allah has already preceded? We say: the benefit in it is what Ṣāḥib al-Kashshāf mentioned, and he did very well in it. He said: the purpose of it is to alert that if Allah were present in the Throne, the bearers of the Throne and those surrounding the Throne would be seeing Him and witnessing Him. And since their belief in the existence of Allah entails praise and commendation, because affirming the existence of a present, seen, witnessed thing does not entail praise and commendation (do you not see that affirming the existence of the sun and that it is luminous does not entail praise and commendation?), when Allah mentioned their belief in Him in the manner of praise, commendation and exaltation, it became known that they believed in Him, as evidenced by the fact that they did not see Him present and sitting there. May Allah have mercy on Ṣāḥib al-Kashshāf; had he not included in his book anything but this point, it would have sufficed him as pride and honour.

The third type of what Allah related about these angels is His saying: ﴿and they ask forgiveness for those who believe.﴾ Know that it is established that complete happiness is tied to two matters: exalting the command of Allah, and compassion toward the creation of Allah. And it is necessary that exalting the command of Allah be prior to compassion toward the creation of Allah. So His saying ﴿they glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him﴾ indicates exalting the command of Allah, and His saying
صفحة ٣٠
﴿and they ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾ indicates compassion toward the creation of Allah.

Then there are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Many scholars have used this verse to establish that the angel is better than the human. They said: this verse indicates that when the angels finished mentioning Allah with praise and sanctification, they occupied themselves with seeking forgiveness for others, namely the believers. This shows that they are independent of seeking forgiveness for themselves; for if they were in need of it, they would have put seeking forgiveness for themselves before seeking forgiveness for others, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Begin with yourself." Also Allah said to Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah, and ask forgiveness for your sin and for the believing men and believing women﴾ [Muhammad: 19]; so He commanded Muhammad to mention first seeking forgiveness for himself, and after that to seek forgiveness for others. And He related of Nuh, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents and whoever enters my house believing, and the believing men and believing women﴾ [Nuh: 28]. This indicates that everyone who is in need of forgiveness puts seeking forgiveness for himself before seeking it for others. So if the angels were in need of forgiveness, their occupation with seeking forgiveness for themselves would have preceded their occupation with seeking it for others. And since Allah did not mention from them their seeking forgiveness for themselves, we know that this was because they were not in need of forgiveness. As for the prophets, peace be upon them, they were in need of forgiveness, based on His saying to Muhammad, peace be upon him: ﴿and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾. And if this is established, then it is clear that the angel is better than the human. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: al-Ka'bi used this verse to establish that the effect of intercession is in the increase of reward for believers, not in removing punishment from sinners. He said: that is because the angels said: ﴿So forgive those who repent and follow Your way﴾. He said: what is meant is not "forgive those who repented from disbelief," whether he was persisting in sin or not, because one whose state is such is not described as following the way of his Lord, and that is not applied to him. Also the angels say: ﴿and admit them into the Gardens of Eden which You have promised them﴾, and this is not fitting for the wicked, because our opponents do not affirm with certainty that Allah promised them Paradise; they only permit that. So it is established that the intercession of the angels only reaches the people of obedience, and so the intercession of the prophets must be the same, since there is no one who makes a distinction. The answer: we say this verse indicates the occurrence of intercession from the angels for sinners. We will explain this, then answer what al-Ka'bi mentioned. As for the explanation of how this verse indicates what we have said, it is from several aspects:

The first: His saying: ﴿and they ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾. Seeking forgiveness is requesting forgiveness, and forgiveness is only mentioned in the removal of punishment. As for requesting an additional benefit, it is not called seeking forgiveness.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they ask forgiveness for those who believe﴾, and this indicates that they seek forgiveness for every people of faith. So when we establish that the person who commits a major sin is a believer, it is necessary that he enter under this intercession.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So forgive those who repent﴾. Requesting forgiveness for those who repent: it is not permissible that what is meant is the removal of punishment for a major sin after repentance, because that is obligatory upon Allah according to the opponent, and what is obligatory in action, asking for it by supplication is ugly. Nor is it permissible that what is meant is the removal of punishment for minor sins, because that too is obligatory, so asking for it by supplication is not fitting. Nor is it permissible that what is meant is requesting an increase in benefit beyond the reward, because that is not called forgiveness. So it is established that His saying ﴿So forgive those who repent﴾ cannot be understood except as the removal of the punishment for a major sin before repentance. And if this is established regarding the angels, then likewise regarding the prophets, since consensus is established that there is no difference. As for what al-Ka'bi relies on, namely that they requested forgiveness for those who repented, we say: it must be that what is meant by it is those who repented from disbelief and followed the way of faith. As for his saying that one who repents from disbelief while persisting in wickedness is not called a penitent nor one who follows the way of Allah, we say: we do not concede his statement; rather it is said: he is a penitent from disbelief and a follower of the way of Allah in religion and law. And when it is established that he is a penitent from disbelief, it is established that he is a penitent. Do you not see that for the truth of describing someone as a striker or a laugher, it suffices that striking or laughing proceeds from him once, and that does not depend on all kinds of striking or laughing proceeding from him? So likewise here.

**Third issue:** The people of verification (*ahl al-tahqiq*) said: This intercession by the angels on behalf of humankind takes the form of an apology for a past lapse. When the angels first learned of the creation of humans, they said: ﴿Will You place in it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30]. After that statement had been made, they made amends in the end by saying: ﴿So forgive those who have repented and followed Your way, and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾. This is like an indication that whoever harms another should preferably compensate for that harm by bringing a benefit to him.

* * *

Know that when the Exalted described the angels as asking forgiveness for those who repent, He explained the manner of that seeking of forgiveness. He related of them that they said: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾. On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Supplication in most matters is mentioned with the words "Our Lord" (*rabbana*). The evidence for this is that the angels, when supplicating, said "Our Lord" (*rabbana*), as in this verse. Adam, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾. Noah, peace be upon him, said: ﴿My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge﴾ [Hud: 47]. He also said: ﴿My Lord, I have called to my people night and day﴾ [Nuh: 5], and said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾ [Nuh: 28]. Of Abraham, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260], and he said: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents and the believers on the day the reckoning takes place﴾ [Ibrahim: 41]. He said: ﴿Our Lord, make us Muslims [submitting] to You, and from our descendants a Muslim nation [submitting] to You﴾ [al-Baqarah: 128]. Of Joseph, He said: ﴿My Lord, You have given me of sovereignty﴾ [Yusuf: 101]. Of Moses, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿My Lord, show me [Yourself] that I may look at You﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]. In the account of the striking, He said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me.' So He forgave him; indeed, He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.' He said: 'My Lord, for that by which You have favored me, I will never be a supporter of the criminals﴾ [al-Qasas: 17]. The Exalted related of Dawud: ﴿So he asked forgiveness of his Lord and fell down bowing and turned in repentance﴾ [Sad: 24]. Of Sulayman, He related that he said: ﴿My Lord, forgive me and grant me a kingdom﴾ [Sad: 35]. Of Zakariyya, that he ﴿called to his Lord in a private call﴾ [Maryam: 3]. Of Isa, peace be upon him, that he said: ﴿Our Lord, send down to us a table [spread with food] from the heaven﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 114]. Of Muhammad (ﷺ), that Allah the Exalted said to him: ﴿And say: My Lord, I seek refuge in You from the incitements of the devils﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 97]. He related of the believers that they said: ﴿Our Lord, You did not create this in vain﴾ [Al 'Imran: 191], and they repeated this expression five times. He also related of them that they said: ﴿Our Lord, [we seek] Your forgiveness, and to You is the destination﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], up to the end of the surah.

It is established from what we have mentioned that among the most pleasing forms of supplication is that the servant call upon his Lord by saying: "O my Lord." The full difficulty in this is to be stated thus: the word "Allah" is greater than the word "Lord" (*al-Rabb*), so why has the word "Lord" become specific to the time of supplication? The answer: It is as if the servant is saying: "I was in the concealment of non-existence, the pure void and absolute negation, and You brought me out into existence and nurtured me. So make Your nurturing of me an intercessor before You, that You not leave me for the blink of an eye without Your nurturing, Your kindness and Your bounty."

[Page 32]

**The second issue:** The sunnah in supplication is that one begins it with praise of Allah the Exalted, and then mentions the supplication immediately after it. The evidence for this is this verse, for when the angels resolved to supplicate and ask forgiveness for the believers, they began with praise, saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾. Also, when Abraham, peace be upon him, wished to mention the supplication, he first mentioned the praise, saying: ﴿He who created me, and it is He who guides me. And it is He who feeds me and gives me drink. And when I am ill, it is He who cures me. And who will cause me to die and then bring me to life. And who I aspire will forgive me my sin on the Day of Recompense﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 78–82]. All of this is praise of Allah the Exalted, and after it he mentioned the supplication, saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me judgement and join me with the righteous﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 83].

* * *

Know that reason also indicates the observance of this order. The remembrance of Allah through praise and glorification, in relation to the essence of the spirit, is like the supreme elixir in relation to copper. Just as a particle of the elixir, when it falls upon a world of copper, turns the whole into pure gold, so too when a particle of the elixir of knowing the majesty of Allah the Exalted falls upon the essence of the rational spirit, it is transformed from the impurity of copper into the purity of holiness and the permanence of the world of purity. It is thus established that when the light of knowledge of Allah the Exalted shines upon the essences of the spirit, the spirit becomes more pure in clarity and more perfect in illumination. When it becomes so, its power becomes stronger and its influence more perfect, so the attainment of the desired thing through supplication becomes nearer and more complete. This is the reason for placing praise of Allah before supplication.

**The third issue:** Know that the angels described Allah the Exalted with three types of attributes: lordship (*al-rububiyyah*), mercy and knowledge. As for lordship, it indicates bringing into existence and originating. There is another subtle point in it: their saying "Our Lord" (*rabbana*) indicates nurturing (*al-tarbiyah*), and nurturing is an expression for keeping a thing in its most perfect condition and its best attributes. This shows that these contingent beings, just as they are in need at the moment of their coming into being of the bringing into existence and origination by the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, so too they are in need, at the moment of their continuance, of Allah's sustaining them. As for mercy, it indicates that the side of goodness, mercy and kindness outweighs the side of harm, and that He, the Exalted, created creation only for mercy and goodness, not for harm and evil.

If it is said: In the saying ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾ there is a problem, because knowledge has encompassed all things, but mercy has not reached all things, since one who is harmed, at the moment he falls into harm, that harm is not mercy. This question is also mentioned in His saying: ﴿My mercy has encompassed all things﴾ [al-A'raf: 156]. We say: Every existent has received a share of the mercy of Allah the Exalted. That is because the existent is either necessary (*wajib*) or contingent (*mumkin*). As for the necessary, there is none but Allah, glorified and exalted is He. As for the contingent, its existence is from Allah the Exalted and by His bringing it into being, and that is mercy. Thus it is established that there is no existent other than Allah except that a portion and an allotment of the mercy of Allah has reached it. Therefore He said: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾.

In the verse there is another subtle point: the angels placed the mention of mercy before the mention of knowledge, saying: ﴿Our Lord, You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾. That is because what they sought was the conveying of mercy and that He pass over what He knew of them of kinds of sins. So the thing sought in itself is mercy, and the thing sought incidentally is that He pass over what He knew of them. What is sought in itself takes precedence over what is sought incidentally.

[Page 33]

Do you not see that, since preserving health is sought in itself and removing sickness is sought incidentally, therefore when they defined medicine (*al-tibb*), they placed in it the preservation of health before the removal of sickness, saying: "Medicine is a science by which the conditions of the human body are known, in terms of what becomes sound and what departs from health, so that health may be preserved when present and restored when lost." Likewise here, the thing sought in itself is mercy, while passing over what He knew of them of kinds of sins is sought incidentally, because the attainment of mercy in its complete form is only achieved through passing over sins. For this reason, the mention of mercy came before the mention of knowledge.

**The fourth issue:** This verse indicates that the principal purpose of the first creation and the bringing into being is mercy, bounty, generosity and nobility. The certain proofs indicate that whatever enters existence of kinds of good and evil, happiness and wretchedness, is by the decree and predestination of Allah. Combining these two principles is extremely difficult. At this point the philosophers said: Good is willed and approved, and evil is willed and disliked. Good is decreed by Him in itself, and evil is decreed by Him incidentally. In this there is a great depth.

**The fifth issue:** His saying ﴿You have encompassed all things in mercy and knowledge﴾ indicates that He, glorified is He, knows all the knowables that have no end, both universals and particulars. Furthermore, if this were not so, there would be no benefit in supplication and entreaty, because if it were permissible for some things to fall outside His knowledge, then, under that assumption, the one supplicating would not know that Allah, glorified is He, knows him and knows his supplication, and under that assumption there would remain no benefit whatsoever in supplication.

Know that when the Exalted related of them the manner of their praise of Allah the Exalted, He related of them the manner of their supplication, which is that they said: ﴿So forgive those who have repented and followed Your way, and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾. Know that the angels requested from Allah the Exalted by way of supplication many things for the believers. The first thing requested is forgiveness, and its explanation has already preceded in His saying: ﴿So forgive those who have repented and followed Your way﴾. If it is said: Forgiveness has no meaning except the removal of punishment, and on this assumption there is no difference between His saying "So forgive them" and His saying ﴿and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾. We say: The indication of the word forgiveness on the removal of the punishment of Hellfire is an indication by way of allusion and suggestion. So when they mentioned this supplication by way of allusion and suggestion, they followed it with its mention by way of explicit statement, for the sake of emphasis and intensification. Know that when they asked Allah to remove punishment from them, they followed it by asking Allah to convey reward to them, saying: ﴿Our Lord, and admit them to the Gardens of Eternity which You have promised them﴾. If it is said: You claim that this intercession occurs only for sinners, and this verse refutes that, because the Exalted did not promise sinners that He would admit them into the Gardens of Eternity. We say: We do not concede that He did not promise them that, because we have shown that the many proofs in the Qur'an indicate that He, the Exalted, does not make eternal in the Fire the people of "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah." And when He brings them out of the Fire, it is necessary that He admit them into Paradise. Thus this constitutes a promise from Allah the Exalted to them that He will admit them into the Gardens of Eternity, either without entering the Fire or after He has made them enter the Fire.

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever was righteous among their fathers, their spouses and their descendants﴾. That is: "And admit along with them into Paradise these three groups, namely the righteous among the fathers, the spouses and the descendants." This is because when a man has with him in the setting of his life and his joy his family and his kin, his delight is more complete. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "Whoever was righteous" (*man salaha*) is in the accusative case from two positions: if you wish, you may refer it back to the pronoun in His saying ﴿and admit them﴾, and if you wish, to the pronoun in ﴿which You have promised them﴾. The meaning of His saying ﴿whoever was righteous﴾ is the people of faith.

Then they said: ﴿Indeed, You, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾. They mentioned these two attributes in their supplication because, if He were not Mighty, but were such that He could be overpowered and prevented, the requested thing could not occur from Him, and if He were not Wise, this requested thing would not be achieved in accordance with wisdom and benefit.

[Page 34]

Then after that they said: ﴿And protect them from evil deeds﴾. Some of them said: The meaning is "protect them from the punishment of evil deeds." If it is said: On this assumption there is no difference between His saying ﴿and protect them from evil deeds﴾ and what preceded of His saying ﴿and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾, and then repetition devoid of benefit would be required, which is impermissible. We say: Rather, the difference arises in two respects. The first: His saying ﴿and protect them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾ is a supplication mentioned for the roots (*usul*), and His saying ﴿and protect them from evil deeds﴾ is a supplication mentioned for the branches (*furu'*).
