**Third issue:** Most of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that denies intercession for sinners) used His saying ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who will be obeyed﴾ to deny intercession for those who commit major sins. They said: He negated that there would be an intercessor for them who would be obeyed, so it must follow that this intercessor will not exist for them. Our companions (ashabuna) answered this in several ways.

The first: He negated that there would be an intercessor for them who is obeyed, and this does not indicate the negation of an intercessor in general. Do you not see that if you say: "I do not have a book that can be sold," this implies the negation of a sellable book, but does not imply the negation of books in general? The Arabs said:

*And you do not see the lizard entering its hole there.*

The word "obeyed" implies that the intercessor has a rank. So this indicates that on the Day of Resurrection there is no intercessor whom Allah obeys, because there is no one in existence of higher status than Allah, the Exalted, such that it could be said that Allah obeys him.

The second answer: The intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" here is the disbelievers. The evidence is that this verse was revealed to rebuke the disbelievers: ﴿those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 35], so it must be specific to them. According to us, there is no intercession for disbelievers.

The third: The word "the wrongdoers" either denotes totality (*istighraq*) or it does not. If it denotes totality, then the intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" is their collective whole, and the disbelievers are included in this collective statement. According to us, this collective has no intercessor, because some of this collective are disbelievers and they have no intercessor; so in that case this collective has no intercessor. If it does not denote totality, then the intended meaning of "the wrongdoers" is some of those described by this attribute, and according to us, some of those described by this attribute have no intercessor, namely the disbelievers.

The proponents (the Mu'tazilah) answered the first objection, saying: The words of Allah must be interpreted in a meaningful way, and everyone knows that there is nothing in existence that Allah obeys, because the one who obeys has a lower status than the one who is obeyed, and there is nothing in existence of higher rank than Allah, the Exalted, such that it could be said that Allah obeys him. And if this meaning is known by necessity, then interpreting the verse in this way removes it from benefit. Therefore "obeyed" must be interpreted as "answered." The evidence that the word "obeyed" can mean "answered" is the saying of the poet:

*How many a man whose chest I have burned with rage, who has wished for my death but was not obeyed.*

As for the second objection, they answered it by saying that the word "wrongdoers" is a plural form preceded by the definite article, which therefore implies generality. At most, the verse was revealed to censure the disbelievers, because the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specific occasion of revelation.

As for the third objection, its answer is that His saying ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend﴾ indicates that each one of the wrongdoers is judged to have no intimate friend and no intercessor who is obeyed. This is the complete statement of the people in establishing that argument.

Our companions answered the first objection, saying: The people used to say about the idols: "They are our intercessors with Allah," and they used to say: "They will intercede for us with Allah without any need for Allah's permission." For this reason Allah refuted them by saying: ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. This indicates that the people believed it was obligatory upon Allah to respond to the idols in that intercession, and this is a kind of obedience. So Allah negated that obedience by His saying: ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who will be obeyed.﴾

[p. 46]

They answered the second statement by saying: The basic function of the definite article is to refer to a known antecedent. When the definite article is attached to a plural form and there is a previously known referent, it refers to that referent. **Fourth issue:** Explaining the composition (*nazm*) of the verse. We say: Allah mentioned in this verse all the causes that necessitate fear. The first is that He called that day "the Day of the Imminent," that is, the day of nearness of His punishment for those who committed a great sin, because when the time of their punishment draws near, they are in the utmost extremity of fear, to the point that it is said that those griefs and anxieties are more frightening than the punishment itself.

The second is His saying ﴿when hearts are at the throats﴾, meaning that the fear reaches such a point that the heart is uprooted from the chest, rises to the throat, clings to it, and blocks the passage of breath.

The third is His saying ﴿choking﴾, meaning they are unable to speak or to express the sorrow and fear they have, and this causes greater anxiety and turmoil.

The fourth is His saying ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who will be obeyed﴾, thus clarifying that they will have no close relative who benefits them, nor an intercessor whose intercession is obeyed on their behalf and accepted.

The fifth is His saying ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾, meaning that He, glory be to Him, is All-Knowing, from whose knowledge not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or the earth is hidden. When a judge reaches this degree of knowledge, the sinner's fear of him becomes extremely intense. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "Treachery" (*khaina*) is an attribute of the glance, or a verbal noun with the meaning of "treacherous," like *al-'afiyah* meaning *al-mu'afah*. The intended meaning is stealing glances at what is not lawful, as people of suspicion do. By His saying "what the breasts conceal" is meant the hidden thoughts of the hearts. The conclusion is that actions are of two kinds: actions of the limbs and actions of the hearts. As for actions of the limbs, the treachery of the eyes conceals them, and Allah knows them; so what then of the rest of the deeds?

And as for the actions of the hearts, they are known to God, Exalted, by His saying: ﴿And He knows what the breasts conceal﴾. This indicates that God, Exalted, has knowledge of all their actions.

The sixth: God's saying, Exalted: ﴿And God judges with truth﴾. This also necessitates great fear, because when a judge has knowledge of all circumstances, and it is established that he judges only with truth in everything minute and great, the fear of the sinner of him is at its utmost extent.

The seventh: the disbelievers relied, in warding off punishment from themselves, on the intercession of these idols, and God, Exalted, made clear that there is absolutely no benefit in them, so He said: ﴿And those whom they invoke besides Him do not decide anything﴾.

The eighth: His saying ﴿Indeed, God is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾, meaning: He hears from the disbelievers their praise of the idols, and does not hear from them their praise of God; and He sees their prostration and submission to them, and does not see their submission
Page 47
and humility before God. So when these eight circumstances are combined regarding the sinner whose sin is great, the warning reaches the limit beyond which no further increase can be conceived. Then, when God, Exalted, had emphasized the warning to the disbelievers with the punishment of the Hereafter, He followed it with an explanation of warning them by the circumstances of this world, and He said: ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ The meaning is that the wise person is one who takes a lesson from others, for those who passed away from the disbelievers were stronger than these present disbelievers, and had greater traces in the land than them, meaning their fortresses, palaces and armies. When they denied their messengers, God destroyed them with various kinds of destruction, swiftly, so that these present disbelievers witness those traces, and God, Exalted, warned them against the like of that by this statement. And He explained by His saying: ﴿And they had no protector from God﴾ that when the punishment descended upon them at the time of God's seizing them, they did not find anyone to help them and deliver them. Then He explained that this descended upon them because they disbelieved and denied the messengers, so He warned the people of the Messenger against the like of it, and concluded the statement by saying that He is ﴿Mighty, severe in punishment﴾, as an intensification of warning and frightening. And God knows best.

Ibn ʿĀmir alone read "kānū hum ashadda minkum" with the kāf, while the rest read it with the hā'. As for the reading of the rest, in the third person, it is for the sake of agreement with the third-person wording preceding it.

The second is His saying ﴿when hearts are at the throats﴾, meaning that the fear reaches such a point that the heart is uprooted from the chest, rises to the throat, clings to it, and blocks the passage of breath.

The third is His saying ﴿choking﴾, meaning they are unable to speak or to express the sorrow and fear they have, and this causes greater anxiety and turmoil.

The second is His saying ﴿when hearts are at the throats﴾, meaning that the fear reaches such a point that the heart is uprooted from the chest, rises to the throat, clings to it, and blocks the passage of breath.

The third is His saying ﴿choking﴾, meaning they are unable to speak or to express the sorrow and fear they have, and this causes greater anxiety and turmoil.

The fourth is His saying ﴿The wrongdoers will have no intimate friend, nor any intercessor who will be obeyed﴾, thus clarifying that they will have no close relative who benefits them, nor an intercessor whose intercession is obeyed on their behalf and accepted.

The fifth is His saying ﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes and what the breasts conceal﴾, meaning that He, glory be to Him, is All-Knowing, from whose knowledge not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or the earth is hidden. When a judge reaches this degree of knowledge, the sinner's fear of him becomes extremely intense. The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: "Treachery" (*khaina*) is an attribute of the glance, or a verbal noun with the meaning of "treacherous," like *al-'afiyah* meaning *al-mu'afah*. The intended meaning is stealing glances at what is not lawful, as people of suspicion do. By His saying "what the breasts conceal" is meant the hidden thoughts of the hearts. The conclusion is that actions are of two kinds: actions of the limbs and actions of the hearts. As for actions of the limbs, the treachery of the eyes conceals them, and Allah knows them; so what then of the rest of the deeds?

And as for the actions of the hearts, they are known to God, Exalted, by His saying: ﴿And He knows what the breasts conceal﴾. This indicates that God, Exalted, has knowledge of all their actions.

The sixth: God's saying, Exalted: ﴿And God judges with truth﴾. This also necessitates great fear, because when a judge has knowledge of all circumstances, and it is established that he judges only with truth in everything minute and great, the fear of the sinner of him is at its utmost extent.

The seventh: the disbelievers relied, in warding off punishment from themselves, on the intercession of these idols, and God, Exalted, made clear that there is absolutely no benefit in them, so He said: ﴿And those whom they invoke besides Him do not decide anything﴾.

The eighth: His saying ﴿Indeed, God is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing﴾, meaning: He hears from the disbelievers their praise of the idols, and does not hear from them their praise of God; and He sees their prostration and submission to them, and does not see their submission

and humility before God. So when these eight circumstances are combined regarding the sinner whose sin is great, the warning reaches the limit beyond which no further increase can be conceived. Then, when God, Exalted, had emphasized the warning to the disbelievers with the punishment of the Hereafter, He followed it with an explanation of warning them by the circumstances of this world, and He said: ﴿Have they not travelled in the land and seen how was the end of those before them?﴾ The meaning is that the wise person is one who takes a lesson from others, for those who passed away from the disbelievers were stronger than these present disbelievers, and had greater traces in the land than them, meaning their fortresses, palaces and armies. When they denied their messengers, God destroyed them with various kinds of destruction, swiftly, so that these present disbelievers witness those traces, and God, Exalted, warned them against the like of that by this statement. And He explained by His saying: ﴿And they had no protector from God﴾ that when the punishment descended upon them at the time of God's seizing them, they did not find anyone to help them and deliver them. Then He explained that this descended upon them because they disbelieved and denied the messengers, so He warned the people of the Messenger against the like of it, and concluded the statement by saying that He is ﴿Mighty, severe in punishment﴾, as an intensification of warning and frightening. And God knows best.

Ibn ʿĀmir alone read "kānū hum ashadda minkum" with the kāf, while the rest read it with the hā'. As for the basis of Ibn ʿĀmir's reading, it is a shift from the third person to the second person, like His saying: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾ [al-Fatiha: 5] after His saying: ﴿Praise be to God﴾ [al-Fatiha: 1]. The reason this address is fitting is that it concerns the people of Mecca, so He made the address follow the wording of the present addressees, given their presence. This verse in meaning is like His saying: ﴿We had established them in the land as We have not established you﴾ [al-An'am: 6]. As for the reading of the rest, in the third person, it is for the sake of agreement with the third-person wording preceding it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 40, verses 23–27:

His saying, exalted is He: "And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a clear authority, to Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and Haman and Qarun, but they said, 'A sorcerer, a liar.' So when he brought them the truth from Us, they said, 'Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women.' And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error." And Fir'awn said, "Leave me, let me kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption in the land." And Musa said, "Indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, consoled His Messenger by mentioning the disbelievers who denied the prophets before him, and by observing the traces of those people, He also consoled him by mentioning Musa, peace be upon him: that despite the great strength of his miracles, He sent him to Fir'awn, Haman and Qarun, and they denied him and opposed him stubbornly, and said, "He is a sorcerer, a liar."

Know that when Musa, peace be upon him, brought them those dazzling miracles and the prophethood, which is what is meant by His saying, "When he brought them the truth from Us," Allah, exalted is He, related what proceeded from them of ignorance. The first: they described him as being a sorcerer, a liar, and this is extremely far-fetched, because those miracles had reached such strength and clarity that every person of sound intellect would witness that they are not from magic at all. The second: they said, "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women." The correct view is that this killing is other than the killing that occurred at the time of Musa's birth, because at that time the astrologers had informed Fir'awn of the birth of an enemy who would prevail over him, so he ordered the killing of the boys at that time. As for this time, Musa had come and displayed the manifest miracles, so at this point he ordered the killing of the sons of those who believed with him, lest they grow up upon the religion of Musa and thereby it would strengthen; and this reason is specific to the sons rather than the daughters, and for this reason he ordered the killing of the sons.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error." Its meaning is that all that they strive for in scheming against Musa and against those who believe with him is nullified, because "whatever mercy Allah grants to people, none can withhold it" [Fatir: 2]. The third type of the ugly deeds of those disbelievers with Musa, peace be upon him, is what Allah, exalted is He, related: "And Fir'awn said, 'Leave me, let me kill Musa.'" This statement is like an indication that they were preventing him from killing him, and in it there are two possibilities:

The first possibility: they prevented him from killing him for several reasons. The first: perhaps there were among them some who believed in their hearts that Musa was truthful, so they devised various stratagems to prevent Fir'awn from killing him. The second: al-Hasan said, his companions said to him, "Do not kill him, for he is merely a weak sorcerer, and he cannot overcome your sorcerers; and if you kill him, you will introduce doubt among the people, and they will say that he was in the right, and they will be unable to answer him, so they will kill him." The third: perhaps they were devising to prevent his killing so that Fir'awn would remain preoccupied with Musa and would not have leisure to discipline those peoples, for it is the nature of rulers to occupy the heart of their king with an external adversary until they become secure from the evil of that king.

The second possibility: that someone prevented Fir'awn from killing Musa, and that he wanted to kill him, but he was afraid that if he attempted to kill him, overpowering miracles would appear preventing him from killing him, and he would be disgraced; yet out of his shamelessness he said, "Leave me, let me kill Musa," and his purpose in saying it was that he refrained from killing him only out of consideration for the hearts of his companions, and his purpose in it was to conceal his fear.

As for his saying, "And let him call upon his Lord," he mentioned it by way of mockery, meaning: I will kill him, so let him say to his Lord that He may rescue him from me.

* * *

As for his saying, "Indeed I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption in the land," there are issues in it:

The first issue: Ibn Kathir opened the ya' in His saying "Leave me" (dharuni), and Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr opened the ya' in "Indeed I fear" (inni akhafu). Also Nafi' and Ibn 'Umar recited "wa-an yuzhiru" (or that they will manifest) with a waw and with the omission of (aw, "or"), meaning that it combines the changing of the religion with the manifesting of corruptions. Those who recited with the form of (aw) mean that one of the two matters must necessarily occur. It was also recited as "yuzhira" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the ha', and (al-fasad, "the corruption") in the accusative as a transitive verb. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited with the wording (aw yazhara) with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', and (al-fasad) in the nominative. As for the rationale of the first reading, it is that He attributed the verb to Musa in His saying "yubaddila" (he changes), so likewise in "yuzhira," so that the speech would be in one pattern. As for the rationale of the second reading, it is that when he changes the religion, the corruption resulting from that change has become manifest.

The second issue: the purpose of this statement is to explain the cause that necessitates his killing, which is that his existence necessitates either the corruption of the religion or the corruption of the world. As for the corruption of the religion, it is because the people believed that the true religion is that which they followed; so when Musa was striving to corrupt it, in their belief he was striving to corrupt the true religion. As for the corruption of the world, it is that a people must gather around him and this becomes a cause for disputes and the stirring up of strife; and since people's love for their religions is above their love for their wealth, Fir'awn undoubtedly began with mention of the religion, saying, "Indeed I fear that he will change your religion," then followed it with mention of the corruption of the world, saying, "or that he will cause corruption in the land."

* * *

Know that when He, exalted is He, related this statement of Fir'awn, He then related what Musa, peace be upon him, said. He related of him that he said: "Indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning." In it there are two issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Abu Bakr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "'udtu" with the dhal assimilated into the ta', and the rest with clear pronunciation.

The second issue: the meaning is that he did not resort, in repelling his evil, except by seeking refuge in Allah and relying upon the bounty of Allah; so, undoubtedly, Allah protected him from every affliction and brought him to every hope. Know that these words which Musa, peace be upon him, spoke contain several benefits:

The first benefit: the word "indi" (indeed I) indicates emphasis, and this indicates that the emphasized and reliable way of repelling evils and calamities from the self is reliance upon Allah and trust in the protection of Allah, exalted is He.

The second benefit: he said, "Indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord." Just as at the time of recitation the Muslim says, "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan," so Allah, exalted is He, safeguards His religion and sincerity from the whispers of the devils of the jinn; likewise, when afflictions and fears come from the devils of mankind, if the Muslim says, "I seek refuge in Allah," then Allah safeguards him from every affliction and fear.

The third benefit: His saying, "Indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord." The meaning is as if the servant says: Indeed Allah, glorified is He, is the One who nurtured me and raised me to the degrees of goodness, and protected me from afflictions, and gave me blessings without limit or count; so since the Master is none but Allah, it is necessary that the intelligent person not turn, in repelling every affliction, except to the preservation of Allah, exalted is He.

The fourth benefit: His saying, "and your Lord," contains an incitement to the people of Musa, peace be upon him, that they should follow him in seeking refuge in Allah; and the meaning in it is that pure, strong souls, when they agree upon one resolve, that influence becomes very strong; and that is the principal reason for performing the prayers in congregation.

The fifth benefit: he did not mention Fir'awn in this supplication, because there had already been a right of upbringing owed to Musa from him in some respects, so he left out specifying him out of regard for that right.

The sixth benefit: that although Fir'awn had displayed that act, there is no benefit in supplicating against Fir'awn specifically; rather, the better course is to seek refuge in Allah in repelling everyone who is described with that attribute, so that every enemy is included, whether he displays that enmity or conceals it.

The seventh benefit: that the factor compelling the undertaking of harming people is two matters: first, that the person be arrogant and hard of heart; second, that he deny resurrection and the Last Day. This is because the arrogant, hard-hearted person may be driven by his nature to harm people; but if he affirms the resurrection and the reckoning, his fear of the reckoning becomes a barrier preventing him from acting upon the requirement of his arrogance. When belief in resurrection and the Last Day does not take root in him, his nature calls him to harm, and the barrier, which is fear of the questioning and the reckoning, is removed; and when the fear of questioning and reckoning is removed, hardness and harm inevitably result.

The eighth benefit: when Fir'awn said, "Leave me, let me kill Musa," he said by way of mockery, "And let him call upon his Lord." Then Musa said: What you mentioned, O Fir'awn, by way of mockery, is the clear religion and the luminous truth; and I call upon my Lord and ask Him to repel your evil from me, and you will see how my Lord overpowers you and how He gives me dominion over you.

Know that whoever has his intellect encompassed by these benefits knows that there is no more upright or correct way to repel the plotting of enemies and to nullify their deception except seeking refuge in Allah and returning to the protection of Allah. And Allah knows best.

As for the corruption of the world, it is that a people must gather around him and this becomes a cause for disputes and the stirring up of strife; and since people's love for their religions is above their love for their wealth, Fir'awn undoubtedly began with mention of the religion, saying, "Indeed I fear that he will change your religion," then followed it with mention of the corruption of the world, saying, "or that he will cause corruption in the land."

* * *

Know that when He, exalted is He, related this statement of Fir'awn, He then related what Musa, peace be upon him, said. He related of him that he said: "Indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning." In it there are two issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Abu Bakr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "'udtu" with the dhal assimilated into the ta', and the rest with clear pronunciation.

The second issue: the meaning is that he did not resort, in repelling his evil, except by seeking refuge in Allah and relying upon the bounty of Allah; so, undoubtedly, Allah protected him from every affliction and brought him to every hope. Know that these words which Musa, peace be upon him, spoke contain several benefits:

The first benefit: the word "indi" (indeed I) indicates emphasis, and this indicates that the emphasized and reliable way of repelling evils and calamities from the self is reliance upon Allah and trust in the protection of Allah, exalted is He.

The second benefit: he said, "Indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord." Just as at the time of recitation the Muslim says, "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan," so Allah, exalted is He, safeguards His religion and sincerity from the whispers of the devils of the jinn; likewise, when afflictions and fears come from the devils of mankind, if the Muslim says, "I seek refuge in Allah," then Allah safeguards him from every affliction and fear.

The third benefit: His saying, "Indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord." The meaning is as if the servant says: Indeed Allah, glorified is He, is the One who nurtured me and raised me to the degrees of goodness, and protected me from afflictions, and gave me blessings without limit or count; so since the Master is none but Allah, it is necessary that the intelligent person not turn, in repelling every affliction, except to the preservation of Allah, exalted is He.

The fourth benefit: His saying, "and your Lord," contains an incitement to the people of Musa, peace be upon him, that they should follow him in seeking refuge in Allah; and the meaning in it is that pure, strong souls, when they agree upon one resolve, that influence becomes very strong; and that is the principal reason for performing the prayers in congregation.

The fifth benefit: he did not mention Fir'awn in this supplication, because there had already been a right of upbringing owed to Musa from him in some respects, so he left out specifying him out of regard for that right.

The sixth benefit: that although Fir'awn had displayed that act, there is no benefit in supplicating against Fir'awn specifically; rather, the better course is to seek refuge in Allah in repelling everyone who is described with that attribute, so that every enemy is included, whether he displays that enmity or conceals it.

This is because the arrogant, hard-hearted person may be driven by his nature to harm people; but if he affirms the resurrection and the reckoning, his fear of the reckoning becomes a barrier preventing him from acting upon the requirement of his arrogance. When belief in resurrection and the Last Day does not take root in him, his nature calls him to harm, and the barrier, which is fear of the questioning and the reckoning, is removed; and when the fear of questioning and reckoning is removed, hardness and harm inevitably result.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 40, verses 23–27:

His saying, exalted is He: "And We certainly sent Musa with Our signs and a clear authority, to Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and Haman and Qarun, but they said, 'A sorcerer, a liar.' So when he brought them the truth from Us, they said, 'Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women.' And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error." And Fir'awn said, "Leave me, let me kill Musa, and let him call upon his Lord. Indeed I fear that he will change your religion or that he will cause corruption in the land." And Musa said, "Indeed I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord from every arrogant one who does not believe in the Day of Reckoning."

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, consoled His Messenger by mentioning the disbelievers who denied the prophets before him, and by observing the traces of those people, He also consoled him by mentioning Musa, peace be upon him: that despite the great strength of his miracles, He sent him to Fir'awn, Haman and Qarun, and they denied him and opposed him stubbornly, and said, "He is a sorcerer, a liar."

Know that when Musa, peace be upon him, brought them those dazzling miracles and the prophethood, which is what is meant by His saying, "When he brought them the truth from Us," Allah, exalted is He, related what proceeded from them of ignorance. The first: they described him as being a sorcerer, a liar, and this is extremely far-fetched, because those miracles had reached such strength and clarity that every person of sound intellect would witness that they are not from magic at all. The second: they said, "Kill the sons of those who believe with him, and spare their women." The correct view is that this killing is other than the killing that occurred at the time of Musa's birth, because at that time the astrologers had informed Fir'awn of the birth of an enemy who would prevail over him, so he ordered the killing of the boys at that time. As for this time, Musa had come and displayed the manifest miracles, so at this point he ordered the killing of the sons of those who believed with him, lest they grow up upon the religion of Musa and thereby it would strengthen; and this reason is specific to the sons rather than the daughters, and for this reason he ordered the killing of the sons.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: "And the plotting of the disbelievers is nothing but in error." Its meaning is that all that they strive for in scheming against Musa and against those who believe with him is nullified, because "whatever mercy Allah grants to people, none can withhold it" [Fatir: 2]. The third type of the ugly deeds of those disbelievers with Musa, peace be upon him, is what Allah, exalted is He, related: "And Fir'awn said, 'Leave me, let me kill Musa.'" This statement is like an indication that they were preventing him from killing him, and in it there are two possibilities:

The first possibility: they prevented him from killing him for several reasons. The first: perhaps there were among them some who believed in their hearts that Musa was truthful, so they devised various stratagems to prevent Fir'awn from killing him. The second: al-Hasan said, his companions said to him, "Do not kill him, for he is merely a weak sorcerer, and he cannot overcome your sorcerers; and if you kill him, you will introduce doubt among the people, and they will say that he was in the right, and they will be unable to answer him, so they will kill him." The third: perhaps they were devising to prevent his killing so that Fir'awn would remain preoccupied with Musa and would not have leisure to discipline those peoples, for it is the nature of rulers to occupy the heart of their king with an external adversary until they become secure from the evil of that king.

The second possibility: that someone prevented Fir'awn from killing Musa, and that he wanted to kill him, but he was afraid that if he attempted to kill him, overpowering miracles would appear preventing him from killing him, and he would be disgraced; yet out of his shamelessness he said, "Leave me, let me kill Musa," and his purpose in saying it was that he refrained from killing him only out of consideration for the hearts of his companions, and his purpose in it was to conceal his fear.
