So do not corrupt your affairs against yourselves, and do not expose yourselves to the might of Allah and His punishment, for you have no power against Him. He said "help us" and "come upon us" because he used to show himself as one of them, and that the one whom he advised was a partner to them in it. When that believer said this speech, ﴿Pharaoh said, "I show you only what I see"﴾, meaning: I do not point you to any opinion other than what I have mentioned, that it is necessary to kill him, to cut off the source of trouble. ﴿And I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾ by this opinion, meaning: the path of righteousness and soundness. Then Allah related that this believer replied to Pharaoh's speech, saying: ﴿I fear for you a day like the day of the factions.﴾

Know that Allah related about that believer that he used to conceal his faith. Now, the one who conceals his faith, how can he be able to utter these words in front of Pharaoh? For this reason, there are two opinions here. The first: when Pharaoh said, ﴿Leave me to kill Musa﴾, that believer did not declare that he was upon the religion of Musa. Rather, he gave the impression that he was with Pharaoh and upon his religion, except that he claimed that the public interest required leaving the killing of Musa, because nothing had proceeded from him except calling to Allah and bringing overpowering miracles, and this does not necessitate killing. Proceeding to kill him would bring upon them being spoken of by people with the vilest words. Rather, it is better to postpone his killing and to prevent him from manifesting his religion, because according to this assessment, if he is a liar, the burden of his lie returns upon him, and if he is truthful, benefit is obtained from him in some respects. Then he emphasized this by his saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar﴾, meaning: if he is truthful in what he claims of affirming the Powerful, Wise God, then He does not guide the transgressing liar. Thus he gave Pharaoh the impression that he meant by his saying ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide one who is a transgressor, a liar﴾ that he meant Musa, whereas he was only aiming at Pharaoh, because the transgressing liar is Pharaoh. The second opinion: the believer of Pharaoh's family was concealing his faith at first. But when Pharaoh said, ﴿Leave me to kill Musa﴾, he removed the concealment, showed that he was upon the religion of Musa, and confronted Pharaoh with the truth.

Know that Allah related from this believer kinds of speech which he mentioned to Pharaoh. The first is his saying: ﴿O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions.﴾ The implied meaning is "like the days of the factions," but when he attributed the day to the factions and explained them as the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud, it then became clear that each faction had a specific day of affliction. So he restricted the plural to mentioning one, since there was no ambiguity. Then he explained his saying ﴿I fear for you a day like the day of the factions﴾ by his saying: ﴿like the custom of the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud.﴾ The "custom" (da'b) of these people, beyond them, in their deeds of disbelief, denial, and all other sins, means that this was constant and perpetual, not ceasing from it. There must be an omitted genitive construction (mudaf mahdhuf, a dropped word that the sentence implies); the meaning is: "like the recompense for their custom." The summary is that he warned them of a swift destruction in this world, and then warned them also of the destruction of the Hereafter, which is his saying: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾ What is intended by it is to alert to the punishment of the Hereafter.

The second of the believer's kinds of speech is the words of Allah Most High: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants.﴾ The meaning is that the destruction of those factions was just, because they deserved it on account of their denial of the prophets. So that sentence stands here, and therefore the ruling must be applied here too. The Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) said: ﴿And Allah does not desire injustice for the servants﴾ indicates that He does not desire that some servants wrong others, and indicates that He does not desire the injustice of any of the servants. So if He created disbelief in them and then punished them for that disbelief, He would be unjust. And when it is established that He does not desire injustice at all, it is established that He is not the creator of the actions of the servants, because if He created them, He would have willed them. It is also established that He is capable of injustice, for if He were not capable of it, praise for abandoning injustice would not occur. This argument we have mentioned many times in this book along with its answer, so there is no benefit in repeating it.

The third of this believer's kinds of speech is his saying: ﴿And O my people, I fear for you the day of calling out.﴾ On this there are several issues.

First issue: al-tanadi (the calling out) is a reciprocal form derived from al-nida' (calling). It is said: "the people called out" (tanada al-qawm), meaning some of them called out to others. The original root has a "ya'" and deleting the "ya'" is good in the endings of verses (fawasil, the rhyming ends of verses). We mentioned this regarding ﴿the day of meeting﴾. The commentators unanimously agreed that ﴿the day of calling out﴾ is the Day of Resurrection. Regarding the reason for naming that day with that name, there are several views. The first: the people of the Fire call out to the people of Paradise, and the people of Paradise call out to the people of the Fire, as Allah mentioned about them in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿And the companions of the Fire will call out to the companions of Paradise﴾ [al-A'raf: 50], ﴿and the companions of Paradise will call out to the companions of the Fire.﴾ The second: al-Zajjaj said: it is not far-fetched that the reason for it is His saying: ﴿The day We will call every people with their leader﴾ [al-Isra': 71]. The third: some of the wrongdoers call out to others with "woe" and "destruction," so they say: ﴿O woe to us!﴾ [al-Anbiya': 97]. The fourth: they will be called out to the place of gathering, i.e., they will be summoned. The fifth: the believer calls out ﴿Here, read my record!﴾ [al-Haqqah: 19], and the disbeliever says ﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my record!﴾ [al-Haqqah: 25]. The sixth: they are called out to with the curse upon the wrongdoers. The seventh: death is brought in the form of a white-spotted ram, then it is slaughtered, and a caller calls: "O people of the Resurrection, there is no death!" So the people of Paradise increase in joy upon their joy, and the people of the Fire in sorrow upon their sorrow. The eighth: Abu Ali al-Farisi said: al-tanadi is derived from al-tanadd, from the saying of people: "so-and-so fled" (nadda fulan) when he ran away. This is the reading of Ibn Abbas, and he explained it, saying: they will flee as camels flee. The validity of this reading is supported by the words of Allah Most High: ﴿The Day a man will flee from his brother﴾ [Abasa: 34], and the verse. And His saying after this verse: ﴿The day you turn back in retreat﴾, because when they hear the roar of the Fire they will flee in headlong flight, and they will not reach any region of the regions except that they find angels in ranks, so they will return to the place where they had been.

Second issue: the phrase ﴿the day of calling out﴾ is in the accusative for two reasons. One: it is an adverb of time (zarf) for "fear," as if he feared for them on that day, because of the punishment that will befall them if they do not believe. The other: the implied meaning is "I fear for you the punishment of the day of calling out." If it is like that, then the accusative of "day" is the accusative of a direct object (maf'ul bihi), not an adverb of time, because its grammatical case is that of the omitted genitive construction. Then he said: ﴿the day you turn back in retreat﴾, which is an apposition (badal) of ﴿the day of calling out.﴾ From Qatada: "turning away from the station of the Day of Reckoning toward the Fire." From Mujahid: "fleeing from the Fire, not able to escape." Then he emphasized the threat, saying: ﴿You will have no protector from Allah,﴾ and then he drew attention to the strength of their misguidance and the severity of their ignorance, saying: ﴿And whomever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide.﴾

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 40, verse 35:**

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Yusuf came to you before with clear proofs, but you remained in doubt about what he brought you, until, when he died, you said, "Allah will never send after him any messenger." Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter.﴾ ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without authority having come to them. It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah and in the sight of those who believe. Thus does Allah seal every heart of arrogant tyrants.﴾

Know that when the believer from the people of Pharaoh said, ﴿And whoever Allah leaves astray, for him there is no guide﴾, he gave an example for this, which is that Yusuf came to them with dazzling clear proofs, but they persisted in doubt and suspicion, and did not benefit at all from those proofs. This indicates that whomever Allah leaves astray, ﴿for him there is no guide.﴾ There are issues in the verse:

**The first issue:** It was said that this Yusuf is Yusuf son of Ya'qub, peace be upon them both. The author of *al-Kashshaf* (*al-Kashshaf*, the tafsir of al-Zamakhshari) reported that he is Yusuf son of Ifraim son of Yusuf son of Ya'qub, who remained among them for a little over twenty years. It was also said that the Pharaoh of Musa is the Pharaoh of Yusuf, who remained alive until his time; and it was said that it is another Pharaoh. The aim of all of this is one thing, which is that Yusuf came to his people with clear proofs. Regarding what is meant by "clear proofs," there are two views. The first: what is meant by the clear proofs is his saying: ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Subduer?﴾ [Yusuf: 39]. The second: what is meant by them is the miracles, and this is more preferable. Then they remained doubtful and suspicious about his prophethood, and did not benefit at all from those clear proofs. So when he died, they said that ﴿Allah will never send after him a messenger.﴾ They only passed this judgment by way of wishful thinking and desire, without any proof or evidence. Rather, they only mentioned that so that it would be a foundation for them to deny the prophets who would come after that. There is nothing in their saying ﴿Allah will never send after him a messenger﴾ meant to confirm the message of Yusuf, for how could it be, when they had doubted it and disbelieved in it? Rather, it is a denial of the message of one who comes after him, added to the denial of his own message. Then He said: ﴿Thus does Allah leave astray whoever is a transgressor and a doubter﴾, meaning: like this misguidance, Allah leaves astray every transgressor in his disobedience, every doubter in his religion. Al-Ka'bi said: this verse is a proof for the Qadariyya (the advocates of human free will against divine predestination), because He, exalted is He, explained their disbelief, then explained that He, exalted is He, only led them astray because they were transgressors and doubters. Thus it is established that the servant, as long as he has not gone astray from the religion, Allah, exalted is He, does not lead him astray.

Then He, exalted is He, explained what caused them to remain in that doubt and transgression, and said: ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah without authority﴾, meaning without proof, but either based on mere imitation (*taqlid*, uncritically following others), or based on contemptible doubts. ﴿It is greatly hateful in the sight of Allah.﴾ *Maqt* (hatred, abhorrence) is when a person reaches a great level of wrongdoing among a people, so Allah hates him, detests him, and makes his disgrace and ruin manifest.

In this are issues:

**The first issue:** In his blaming them for disputing without authority is an indication that disputing with proof is good and true, and in it is a refutation of imitation.

**The second issue:** The Qadi (al-Qadi) said: Allah's hatred of them indicates that their act is not created by Allah, because His being the doer of the act and also the one who hates it is impossible.

**The third issue:** The verse indicates that it is permissible to describe Allah, exalted is He, as hating some of His servants. However, that is an attribute that must be interpreted (*ta'wil*, figurative interpretation) with respect to Allah, like anger, shame, and wonder. And Allah knows best. Then He explained that this hatred, just as it occurred in the sight of Allah, similarly occurred in the sight of those who believe.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Thus does Allah seal every heart of arrogant tyrants﴾. In this are issues:

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Qutayba, from al-Kisa'i, read *qalbin* with tanwin (nunation), and *mutakabbirin* as an adjective of *qalb*. The rest read it without tanwin, with the *qalb* construct-annexed to *mutakabbir*. Abu 'Ubayd said: the preferred reading is the annexation (*idafa*), for several reasons. The first: 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read ﴿upon every heart of an arrogant one﴾, and this supports this reading. The second: describing a human being with arrogance and tyranny is better than describing the heart with them. As for those who read with tanwin, they said: arrogance has been annexed to the heart in His saying: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but pride﴾ [Ghafir: 56], and He, exalted is He, said: ﴿his heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283]. Also, it is possible that this is by omitting the annexed noun, meaning "upon every one who has a heart that is arrogant." Also, some people said: the true human being is the heart. This discussion is lengthy, and we have mentioned it in the tafsir of His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193]. They said: whoever annexes must have an omitted element, and the meaning is: "Allah seals the heart of every arrogant one."

**The second issue:** The discussion of sealing (*tab'*), covering (*rayn*), hardness (*qaswa*) and veiling (*ghisha*) has preceded in this book in detail. Our companions (the Ash'aris) say that His saying ﴿Thus does Allah seal﴾ indicates that all of it is from Allah. The Mu'tazila say that His saying ﴿Thus does Allah seal every heart of arrogant tyrants﴾ indicates that this sealing occurred from Allah because he was in himself arrogant and a tyrant. At this point the verse becomes a proof for each of these two groups in one respect, and against them in another respect. The view that reconciles both aspects is what we have adopted, which is that He, exalted is He, creates the motives of arrogance and leadership in the heart, so these motives become a barrier preventing the occurrence of what would call to obedience and submission to Allah's command. Thus the doctrine of divine decree and destiny (*qada' wa qadar*) is sound, and the explanation of turning away from religion by being domineering and arrogant remains valid. Thus it is established that this doctrine that we have chosen regarding divine decree and destiny is the one with which the wording of the Qur'an fits from its beginning to its end.

**The third issue:** It is necessary to explain the difference between *mutakabbir* (arrogant) and *jabbar* (tyrant). Muqatil said: "*mutakabbir*" means arrogant toward accepting monotheism, and "*jabbar*" means tyrannical without right. I say: the perfection of happiness lies in two matters: glorifying Allah's command, and compassion toward Allah's creation. So according to Muqatil's view, arrogance is like the opposite of glorifying Allah's command, and tyranny is like the opposite of compassion toward Allah's creation. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 40, verses 36–42 (part 1 of 2):

The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Pharaoh said, "O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways, the ways of the heavens, and look upon the God of Moses. Indeed, I think him a liar." And thus was the evil of his deeds made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the (right) path. And the plot of Pharaoh was nothing but in ruin.﴾

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, described Pharaoh as arrogant and tyrannical, He explained that he had reached such a degree of stupidity and foolishness that he intended to ascend to the heavens. In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: A large number of the Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) have used this verse as evidence that Allah is in the heavens, and they established this from several angles.

The first angle: Pharaoh was among those who denied the existence of Allah. Everything he said about the attributes of Allah, he said only because he had heard that Moses described Allah in that way, so he too repeated it as he had heard it. Had he not heard Moses describe Allah as existing in the heaven, he would not have sought Him in the heaven.

The second angle: He said, "And indeed I think him a liar," and he did not specify in what he was a liar. The previous mention is what determines the direction of the speech. So the implied meaning is: "I will look at the God whom Moses claims exists in the heaven." Then he said, "And indeed I think him a liar," meaning: "And indeed I think Moses a liar in his claim that God exists in the heaven." This shows that the religion of Moses is that God exists in the heaven.

The third angle: The knowledge that if a god existed, he would be in the heaven, is a self-evident knowledge established in all minds. For this reason, when children supplicate to Allah they raise their faces and hands to the sky. And Pharaoh, despite the extreme of his disbelief, when he sought the god, sought him in the heaven. This shows that the knowledge that God exists in the heaven is a knowledge established in the intellect of the truthful and the heretic, the atheist and the zindiq (heretic), the learned and the ignorant.

This is the whole of the Mushabbihah's proofs from this verse. The answer is: these ignorant people are sufficiently disgraced and misguided in that they made the saying of the accursed Pharaoh a proof for the validity of their religion. As for Moses, peace be upon him, he did not add to the description of the Lord of the worlds beyond the attribute of creating. He said in Surah Ta-Ha: ﴿Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation, then guided it﴾ [Ta-Ha: 50], and he said in Surah al-Shu'ara: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones﴾ ﴿Lord of the east and the west and whatever is between them﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 26–28]. It is thus clear that defining the essence of Allah by His being in the heaven is the religion of Pharaoh, and defining Him by creating and existence is the religion of Moses. So whoever holds the first is upon the religion of Pharaoh, and whoever holds the second is upon the religion of Moses.

Then we say: We do not concede that everything Pharaoh said about the attributes of Allah, the Exalted, he heard from Moses, peace be upon him. Rather, it is possible that he was upon the belief of the Mushabbihah, so he believed that if God existed He would be located in the heaven. Thus he mentioned this belief from himself, not because he had heard it from Moses, peace be upon him.

* * *

As for His saying, ﴿And indeed I think him a liar﴾, we say: Perhaps when he heard Moses, peace be upon him, say, ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 102], he thought that by it he meant that He is the Lord of the heavens, just as one of us is said to be "the lord of the house" meaning that he dwells in it. When this became dominant in his thought, he related it from him. This is not far-fetched, for Pharaoh had reached such a degree of ignorance and foolishness that it is not unlikely that this fancy be attributed to him. If the opponent finds it far-fetched to attribute this fancy to him, that would be fitting for them, because since they are upon the religion of Pharaoh, it is obligatory for them to revere him.

As for his saying that the innate nature (fitrah) of Pharaoh testified that God, if He existed, would be in the heaven, we say: We do not deny that the innate nature of most people makes them imagine the validity of this, especially one who reached the degree of foolishness of Pharaoh. Thus it is established that this argument falls.

The second issue: People differed as to whether Pharaoh intended to build the tower in order to ascend from it to the heaven or not. As for the literalist exegetes, they affirmed this definitively, and they mentioned a lengthy narrative about how that tower was built. What I hold is that this is far-fetched. The proof for this is that one may say: Pharaoh is either one of the insane or one of the sane. If we say he was insane, then it is not permissible from Allah, the Exalted, to send a Messenger to him, because reason is a condition of legal responsibility (taklif), and it is not permissible for Allah to mention the speech of a madman in the Qur'an. But if we say he was among the sane, then we say: every sane person knows by the immediacy of his reason that it is impossible for human power to construct a building higher than the lofty mountain. He also knows by the immediacy of his reason that the appearance of the sky does not differ in sight whether one looks at it from the bottom of the mountains or from the tops of the mountains. When these two pieces of knowledge are self-evident, it is impossible for a sane person to intend to build a structure from which he would ascend to the heaven. And when the corruption of this is known by necessity, it is impossible to attribute it to Pharaoh.

What I hold regarding the interpretation of this verse is that Pharaoh was one of the Dahriyyah (materialists who deny a Creator) and his purpose in mentioning this statement was to raise a doubt about the denial of the Creator. Its formulation is that he said: "We do not see anything that we can judge to be the God of the worlds, so the establishment of this God is impermissible." As for the fact that we do not see Him, it is because if He existed He would be in the heaven, and we have no way to ascend the heavens, so how can we see Him? Then, for the sake of emphasizing that it is not possible for him to ascend the heavens, he said: ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower that I may reach the ways, the ways...﴾. The point is that when everyone knows that this path is impossible, reaching the knowledge of the existence of Allah by way of the senses is impossible, [Page 58] and a parallel to this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a ladder into the sky and bring them a sign...﴾ [al-An'am: 35]. It does not mean that Muhammad ﷺ sought a tunnel in the earth or placed a ladder to the sky. Rather the meaning is that when it is known that this matter is impossible, it is known that there is no way for you to achieve that aim. Likewise here, the aim of Pharaoh in his saying, ﴿O Haman, build for me a tower﴾, means that looking upon the God of Moses, since there was no way to it except by this means, and this means being impossible, then it becomes evident that there is no way to knowing the God whom Moses affirms. This is what I have gathered on this subject.

Know that this doubt is corrupt, because the sources of knowledge are three: sensory perception, report (khabar), and reflection (nazar). The absence of one source, which is sensory perception, does not necessarily entail the absence of what is sought. This is because Moses, peace be upon him, had explained to Pharaoh that the way to knowing Allah, the Exalted, is only through proof and evidence, as he said: ﴿Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones﴾ ﴿Lord of the east and the west﴾ (al-Shu'ara: 26–28). But Pharaoh, through his wickedness and deceit, ignored that proof and presented to the ignorant the notion that since there is no way except sensory perception of this God, it must be denied. This is what I hold on this subject, and with Allah is success and protection.

The third issue: Some people held that Allah, the Exalted, created the substances of the celestial spheres and their motions in such a way that they are the causes (asbab) for the occurrence of events in this lower world. They argued with His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that I may reach the ways, the ways of the heavens﴾, and it is known that they are not causes except for the events of this world. They said: This is reinforced by His saying, the Exalted, in Surah Sad: ﴿Then let them ascend by the causes﴾ [Sad: 10]. As for the exegetes, in explaining His saying, the Exalted, ﴿that I may reach the ways, the ways of the heavens﴾, they said that what is meant by "the ways of the heavens" are their paths and their gates and what leads to them, and whatever brings you to something is a cause (sabab), like guidance and the like.

The fourth issue: The Jews said: The researchers into the histories of the Children of Israel and Pharaoh agree that Haman did not exist at all in the time of Moses and Pharaoh, but came long after them, in a great age and a long epoch. So the claim that Haman existed in the time of Pharaoh is an error in history. And it is no argument for one to say that the existence of a person named Haman after the time of Pharaoh does not prevent the existence of another person with this name in his time. They said: This is because this person named Haman who existed in the time of Pharaoh was not a lowly person in the presence of Pharaoh, but was like his vizier, and a person of this kind cannot be of unknown description and appearance; so had he existed, his condition would have been known. And since the researchers into the conditions of Pharaoh and Moses agree that the person named Haman did not exist in the time of Pharaoh, but came after him by ages, it is known that this is an error that occurred in the histories. They said: A parallel to this is that we know in the religion of Islam that Abu Hanifah came after Muhammad ﷺ. So if someone claimed that Abu Hanifah existed in the time of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and asserted that he was another person apart from the first, who was also called Abu Hanifah, the historians would definitively declare his error. So it is likewise here.

The answer: The histories of Moses and Pharaoh have been long ago, and the conditions and epochs have been disturbed, so there is no reliance on the words of the historians in this matter. Therefore, holding to the word of Allah, the Exalted, is more fitting. This differs from the case of our Messenger with Abu Hanifah, for those histories are recent, not disturbed, rather they are well-preserved. Thus the difference between the two matters is evident. This is the whole of what pertains to the semantic (ma'nawi) discussions in this verse, and what remains is what pertains to the linguistic (lafzi) discussions.

It has been said: "al-Sarh" (the palace/tower) is a conspicuous building that is not hidden from the observer even if he is far away; they derived it from "sarh al-shay'" when a thing becomes manifest. And "asbab al-samawat" means its paths. If it is asked: What is the benefit of this repetition? Had it been said, "that I may reach the ways of the heavens," it would have been sufficient. The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) answered this, saying: When a thing is left vague and then clarified, that is a magnification of its importance. So when he wanted to magnify the ways of the heavens, he left them vague and then clarified them.

As for His saying, ﴿then I may look upon the God of Moses﴾: Hafs, from Asim, read "fa-attali'a" (فَأطَّلِعَ) with a fatha on the ʿayn, and the rest read it with a damma (raf'). Al-Mubarrad said: Whoever reads it in the raised form has made it conjoined (ʿatf) to His saying, "ublugh" (أبْلُغُ), and the sense is: "that I may reach the ways, then look." Yet the particle "thumma" (then) is more delayed than the particle "fa." Whoever reads it in the accusative makes it a response (jawab), and the meaning is: "that I may reach the ways, so when I reach them, I will look." The meaning differs, because the first means: "that I may look," while the second means: "that I may reach," and I guarantee that whenever I reach it, I must look.

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, related this story about Pharaoh, He said after it: ﴿And thus was the evil of his deeds made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred from the (right) path﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "wa-suddda" (وَصُدَّ) with a damma on the sad (ṣ). Abu Ubaydah said: It is read thus, because what precedes it is a verb in the passive voice, so he made what is conjoined to it similar to it. The rest read "wa-sadda" (وَصَدَّ) with a fatha on the sad, on the basis that he prevented people from faith. They said: From his barring is His saying, ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet﴾ [al-A'raf: 124]. This reading is supported by His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved and barred (others) from the path of Allah﴾, and His saying: ﴿They are the ones who disbelieved and barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Fath: 25].

The second issue: His saying, ﴿Was made fair-seeming﴾, requires one who makes it fair-seeming. The Mu'tazilah said: it is Satan. It was said to them: if the one who made Pharaoh's deed fair-seeming is Satan, then the one who made Satan's deed fair-seeming, if it is another devil, necessitates the affirmation of an infinite regress (tasalsul) among the devils or a circular chain (dawr), and that is impossible. Since this is void, it is necessary that the chains of causes and effects end at the Necessary Existent (wajib al-wujud), in the ranks of dependencies. Also, His saying ﴿was made fair-seeming﴾ indicates that if a thing is not, in the belief of the doer, described as good, adornment and beauty, then he does not undertake it. However, if that belief is correct, it is knowledge, and if it is erroneous, it is ignorance. The doer of that ignorance is not that human being, because the rational person does not intend to acquire ignorance for himself, and because he only intends to acquire ignorance for himself if he knows it to be ignorance, and whenever he knows it to be ignorance, it is impossible for him to remain ignorant. Thus it is established that the doer of that ignorance is not that human being. It is not permissible that its doer be Satan, because the first inquiry applies to him in exactly the same way. Nothing remains except that its doer is Allah, the Exalted. And Allah knows best.

If the opponent finds it far-fetched to attribute this fancy to him, that would be fitting for them, because since they are upon the religion of Pharaoh, it is obligatory for them to revere him.

He also knows by the immediacy of his reason that the appearance of the sky does not differ in sight whether one looks at it from the bottom of the mountains or from the tops of the mountains. When these two pieces of knowledge are self-evident, it is impossible for a sane person to intend to build a structure from which he would ascend to the heaven. And when the corruption of this is known by necessity, it is impossible to attribute it to Pharaoh.

What I hold regarding the interpretation of this verse is that Pharaoh was one of the Dahriyyah (materialists who deny a Creator) and his purpose in mentioning this statement was to raise a doubt about the denial of the Creator. This differs from the case of our Messenger with Abu Hanifah, for those histories are recent, not disturbed, rather they are well-preserved. Thus the difference between the two matters is evident. This is the whole of what pertains to the semantic (ma'nawi) discussions in this verse, and what remains is what pertains to the linguistic (lafzi) discussions.

This is not far-fetched, for Pharaoh had reached such a degree of ignorance and foolishness that it is not unlikely that this fancy be attributed to him. If the opponent finds it far-fetched to attribute this fancy to him, that would be fitting for them, because since they are upon the religion of Pharaoh, it is obligatory for them to revere him.

As for his saying that the innate nature (fitrah) of Pharaoh testified that God, if He existed, would be in the heaven, we say: We do not deny that the innate nature of most people makes them imagine the validity of this, especially one who reached the degree of foolishness of Pharaoh. As for the literalist exegetes, they affirmed this definitively, and they mentioned a lengthy narrative about how that tower was built. What I hold is that this is far-fetched. If we say he was insane, then it is not permissible from Allah, the Exalted, to send a Messenger to him, because reason is a condition of legal responsibility (taklif), and it is not permissible for Allah to mention the speech of a madman in the Qur'an. He also knows by the immediacy of his reason that the appearance of the sky does not differ in sight whether one looks at it from the bottom of the mountains or from the tops of the mountains. When these two pieces of knowledge are self-evident, it is impossible for a sane person to intend to build a structure from which he would ascend to the heaven. And when the corruption of this is known by necessity, it is impossible to attribute it to Pharaoh.

What I hold regarding the interpretation of this verse is that Pharaoh was one of the Dahriyyah (materialists who deny a Creator) and his purpose in mentioning this statement was to raise a doubt about the denial of the Creator. This is what I have gathered on this subject.

Know that this doubt is corrupt, because the sources of knowledge are three: sensory perception, report (khabar), and reflection (nazar). So the claim that Haman existed in the time of Pharaoh is an error in history. Therefore, holding to the word of Allah, the Exalted, is more fitting. This differs from the case of our Messenger with Abu Hanifah, for those histories are recent, not disturbed, rather they are well-preserved. Thus the difference between the two matters is evident. This is the whole of what pertains to the semantic (ma'nawi) discussions in this verse, and what remains is what pertains to the linguistic (lafzi) discussions.

The doer of that ignorance is not that human being, because the rational person does not intend to acquire ignorance for himself, and because he only intends to acquire ignorance for himself if he knows it to be ignorance, and whenever he knows it to be ignorance, it is impossible for him to remain ignorant. The essence of the speech is that the Hereafter is lasting and enduring, while this world is finite and perishable, and what endures is better than what ends. Some of the knowers said: If this world were perishing gold and the Hereafter were enduring pottery, the Hereafter would be better than this world; so how much more so when this world is perishing pottery and the Hereafter is enduring gold.

Know that just as the bliss in the Hereafter is everlasting, so too the punishment in it is everlasting, and that encouragement toward everlasting bliss and warning against everlasting punishment are among the strongest aspects of encouragement and warning. Then he explained how recompense occurs in the Hereafter, and he indicated that the side of mercy prevails over the side of punishment, so he said: "Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like." We say: the disbeliever believes in his disbelief that it is obedience and faith; for this reason the disbeliever is resolved to remain persistent in that belief forever. Therefore his punishment is necessarily everlasting, unlike the sinner, who believes his act to be treachery and disobedience, and so is resolved

not to remain persistent in it. Therefore we say that the punishment of the sinner is finite. As for what the Mu'tazilah say, that his punishment is everlasting, it is false, because the duration of that disobedience is finite, and the resolve to commit it again is also not permanent but temporary; so matching it with an everlasting punishment would be contrary to His saying: "Whoever does an evil deed will not be recompensed except with its like."

Know that this verse is a great foundation in the sciences of the Sharia concerning the rulings on crimes (jinayat), for it requires that equivalence be prescribed and that what exceeds the equivalent be not prescribed. Then we say: the verse does not explain in respect of which matters that equivalence is to be observed. If we interpret it as observing equivalence in some specific matter, while that specific matter is not mentioned in the verse, the verse becomes mujmal (general and unclear). Then we say: when He, may He be exalted, explained that the recompense for an evil deed is restricted to its like, He explained that the recompense for a good deed is not restricted to its like, but rather lies beyond reckoning, so He said: "Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer, those will enter Paradise, being provided for therein without account." Our companions (the Ash'arites) argued from this verse, saying: His saying "whoever does righteousness" is an indefinite noun in the context of a conditional, in affirmative form, so it operates like saying: "whoever utters a word, or takes a step, for him is such-and-such." It includes everyone who performs that word or that step even once. Likewise here, it must be said: everyone who does one righteous deed among the righteous deeds enters Paradise and is provided for therein without account. Whoever brings faith and persists in monotheism and sanctification for a period of eighty years has performed the greatest of righteous deeds and the finest of acts of obedience, so he must enter Paradise. The opponent says that he will remain eternally in the Fire forever and ever, and that is contrary to this explicit text. The Mu'tazilah said: He, may He be exalted, stipulated in it that he be a believer, and the perpetrator of a major sin is not a believer according to us, so he does not enter this promise. Others said: because He gives them the reward of their deeds and adds to that reward from the kinds of bounty that lie beyond reckoning. His saying "without account" stands in contrast to "except its like," meaning that the recompense for an evil deed has a reckoning and measure, lest it exceed what is deserved; but the recompense for a righteous deed is without measure or reckoning, rather whatever increase, abundance and expansion beyond what is due you wish. I say: this indicates that the side of mercy and grace prevails over the side of subjugation and punishment. Then that believer resumed and called out a third time, saying: "O my people, what is [wrong] with me that I invite you to salvation while you invite me to the Fire?" The meaning: I invite you to the faith that necessitates salvation, while you invite me to disbelief that necessitates the Fire. If it is asked: why did he repeat the address to his people, and why did he use the conjunction "wa" (and) in the third address but not in the second? We say: as for the repetition of the address, it carries an added alert for them and an awakening from the slumber of heedlessness, and a demonstration that he has increased concern for this important matter and excessive compassion toward those people. As for the use of the conjunctive "wa", the second is nearly identical to the first, since the second is an explanation of the first, and explanation is the same as what is explained. The third, however, is a statement distinct from the first and second, so it is appropriate to introduce the conjunctive "wa" in it. When this believer mentioned that he calls them to salvation while they call him to the Fire, he explained that by saying they call him to disbelief in Allah and to associating partners with Him. As for disbelief in Allah, it is because most of Pharaoh's people denied the existence of God, and some of them acknowledged the existence of Allah but affirmed the worship of idols. His saying, "and associate with Him that of which I have no knowledge," the intended meaning of negating knowledge is negating the known object, as if he said: "and associate with Him that which is not a god." And that which is not a god, how can it be conceived to make it a partner to God?

Since he explained that they call him to disbelief and association, he explained that he calls them to belief in "the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving." His saying "the Exalted in Might" points to His being of perfect power, and contains an alert that the God is He who is of perfect power. As for Pharaoh, he is in extreme helplessness, so how could he be a god? As for the idols, they are carved stones, so how can it be conceived that they are gods? His saying "the Forgiving" points to the fact that they need not despair of the mercy of Allah because of their persistence in disbelief for a long period. For the Lord of the worlds, though He is Mighty and cannot be overcome, Powerful and cannot be vanquished, is also Forgiving, who forgives seventy years of disbelief with one hour of faith.

Then that believer said: "Certainly" (la jarama). The discussion of the meaning of la jarama passed in Surat Hud in His saying: "Certainly, in the Hereafter they will be the greatest losers" [11:22]. The author of al-Kashshaf has repeated it here, saying: "la jarama" — its structure according to the school of the Basrans is that "la" is a rejection of what his people invited him to, and "jarama" is a verb meaning "it is true/it is necessary," and "anna-ma" with what is in its scope is its subject, meaning: it is true, and the nullity of his call is necessary. Or it means "gained," from His saying: "Let not the hatred of a people, because they barred you from the Sacred Mosque, lead you to transgress" [5:2], meaning that the gain of that call to it is the nullity of its call, in the sense that nothing came from it except the manifestation of its nullity. This is all the words of the author of al-Kashshaf.

Then he said: "There is no doubt that what you invite me to has no call in this world or in the Hereafter." The intended meaning is that the idols to whose worship you call me have no call in this world or in the Hereafter. In explaining this "call" there are two possibilities:

Then he said: "and that our return is to Allah," thereby clarifying that these idols have no benefit whatsoever, and with that...

Then indeed our return is to Allah, the All-Knowing of all that is known, the All-Powerful over all that is possible, the Self-Sufficient free of all needs, to whom the word is not changed, and He is not unjust to the servants. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of the servants.﴾ That is, He is Knowing of their conditions and of the measures of their needs. Our companions (the Ash'arites) relied upon His saying Most High: ﴿And I entrust my affair to Allah⁠﴾ to show that everything is from Allah. They said: the Mu'tazilites, who claim that good and evil occur by their own power, have entrusted the affair of their own selves to themselves and did not entrust them to Allah. The Mu'tazilites relied upon this verse and said: His saying ﴿I entrust⁠﴾ is an acknowledgment that he is an independent agent of the act. The discussions mentioned under His saying ﴿I seek refuge in Allah⁠﴾ return in full to this place. Here ends the speech of the believer of the family of Pharaoh. And Allah is the Guide.

Hamzah read "ḥāqa" (حِيقَ) with a kasrah on the ḥāʾ, and so in every place in the Qur'an, while the rest read it with a fatḥah.

As for His saying ﴿The Fire—they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) used this verse to establish the punishment of the grave. They said: the verse requires that the Fire be presented to them morning and evening, and the intended meaning is not the Day of Resurrection, because He said: ﴿and on the Day the Hour will be established: "Admit the people of Pharaoh into the most severe torment."﴾ Nor is the intended meaning the worldly life, because the presentation of the Fire to them morning and evening did not occur in the world. Thus it is established that this presentation occurred after death and before the Day of Resurrection, and this indicates the establishment of the punishment of the grave for these people. When it is established for them, it is established for others, since there is no one who makes a distinction. If it is said: why can the intended meaning of the presentation of the Fire to them morning and evening not be the presentation of admonitions to them in the world? Because when the people of religion mention to them the promise and the warning and frighten them with the punishment of God, they have presented the Fire to them. We then say: there is in the verse what prevents taking it as the punishment of the grave, and its explanation is from two aspects. The first: that punishment must be constant and uninterrupted, while His saying ﴿they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ implies that the punishment occurs only at these two times, so it is established that this cannot be taken as the punishment of the grave. The second: that morning and evening occur only in the world; in the grave there is no existence of them. Thus by these two aspects it is established that this verse cannot be taken as referring to the punishment of the grave.

The answer to the first question: in the world, words were presented to them that remind them of the matter of the Fire, not that the Fire itself was presented to them. So according to their view, the meaning of the verse becomes: the words reminding of the matter of the Fire were presented to them, and this leads to abandoning the apparent wording and turning to metaphor. As for his saying: the verse indicates the occurrence of this punishment at these two times, and that is not permissible, we say: why is it not permissible that it suffices in the grave to deliver the punishment to him at these two times, and then, at the establishment of the Resurrection, he is cast into the Fire, and his punishment continues after that? Also, it is not impossible that the mention of morning and evening is a metaphor for permanence, like His saying: ﴿And for them their provision therein morning and evening﴾. As for his saying that there is no morning and evening in the grave or in the Resurrection, we say: why is it not permissible to say that at the occurrence of these two times for the people of the world, the punishment is presented to them? And Allah knows best.

The second issue: Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read (Admit the people of Pharaoh) (أدْخِلُوا آلَ فِرْعَوْنَ), meaning it is said to the keepers of Hell: "Admit them into the severest torment." The rest read (ادْخُلُوا) (Enter), in the sense that it is said to these disbelievers: "Enter the severest torment." The first reading is the choice of Abu 'Ubaydah, who argued for it with His saying ﴿they are exposed﴾, meaning this is done to them, and so likewise (admit). As for the basis of the second reading, it is His saying ﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾. Here ends the discussion of the story of the believer of the family of Pharaoh.

Know that when the discussion of that story led to explaining the conditions of the Fire, Allah therefore mentioned after it the story of the disputes that take place among the people of the Fire between the leaders and the followers. He said: ﴿And when they argue within the Fire﴾. The meaning is: mention, O Muhammad, to your people when they argue, that is, some of them dispute with others. Then he explained their dispute: the weak say to the leaders ﴿Indeed, we were your followers﴾ in the world. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "tabaʿan" is like khadam, the plural of khādim, or it is of the form dhawī tabaʿ, meaning followers, or it is a description with the verbal noun. ﴿So will you relieve us of a portion of the Fire?﴾ meaning: will you, O leaders, be able to ward off from us a portion of the punishment? Know that those followers know that those leaders have no power to grant that lightening, and their purpose in this speech is only to exaggerate in shaming those leaders and wounding their hearts, because they are the ones who strove to bring these followers into various kinds of misguidance. At this point the leaders say ﴿Indeed, we are all within it﴾, meaning that all of us are subject to this punishment, so if I were able to remove the punishment from you I would remove it from myself. Then they say: ﴿Indeed, Allah has judged between the servants﴾, meaning He conveys to each one the measure of his right of bliss or of punishment. At this point the followers despair of their leaders, so they return to the keepers of Hell and say to them: ﴿Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the torment.﴾ If it is asked: why did He not say: "And those in the Fire said to its keepers," but rather said: ﴿And those in the Fire said to the keepers of Hell﴾? We say there are two answers:

The first: that the purpose of mentioning Hell is to magnify and make the matter terrible. The second: that Jahannam is the name of a place which is the deepest part of the Fire, from their saying: "a well jahannam," meaning of great depth, and in it are the greatest categories of disbelievers in punishment, and the keepers of that place will be the highest in rank among the keepers of Hell before Allah. When the disbelievers know that the matter is so, they seek help from them. Those angels say to them ﴿Did there not come to you your messengers with clear proofs?﴾ The point is that before the sending of messengers the people could say ﴿there came to us no bringer of good tidings or warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19]. But after the coming of the messengers there remains no excuse or pretext, as He said: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15]. This verse indicates that obligation is not realized except after the coming of the law.

Then those angels say to the disbelievers: "Call upon Him yourselves, for we do not dare to do that, and we do not intercede except under two conditions: one of them is that the one for whom intercession is made is a believer, and the second is that permission for intercession has been given." Neither of these two conditions exists, so our undertaking this intercession is impossible. "But call upon Him yourselves." Their saying "Call" is not for hope of benefit, but to indicate disappointment, for if the near angel's supplication is not heard, how will the supplication of the disbelievers be heard? Then they openly tell them that their supplication has no effect, so they say ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ If it is said: need is impossible for God, and if that is so, it is impossible to say that He was harmed by these criminals because of their crime; and if being harmed is impossible for Him, then the desire for vengeance is impossible for Him. If this is established, we say: inflicting these great harms upon those disbelievers is harm with no benefit in it for God the Exalted nor for any of the servants. It is therefore harm empty of every beneficial aspect. How, then, is it fitting for the Merciful, the Generous, to keep that pain forever and ever, without having mercy on their need, without hearing their supplication, and without turning to their humility

Page 66
and brokenness? Even if the hardest-hearted of people did such torment to some of his servants, his generosity and mercy would invite him to pardon them, although this master is in the place of benefit, harm, and need. How, then, is such harm fitting for the Most Generous of the generous? We say: the acts of God are not subject to causal explanation, and "He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned" [al-Anbiya': 23]. So when the true judgment came regarding this in the true Book, it became obligatory to affirm it. And Allah knows best what is correct.

As for His saying ﴿The Fire—they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) used this verse to establish the punishment of the grave. They said: the verse requires that the Fire be presented to them morning and evening, and the intended meaning is not the Day of Resurrection, because He said: ﴿and on the Day the Hour will be established: "Admit the people of Pharaoh into the most severe torment."﴾ Nor is the intended meaning the worldly life, because the presentation of the Fire to them morning and evening did not occur in the world. Thus it is established that this presentation occurred after death and before the Day of Resurrection, and this indicates the establishment of the punishment of the grave for these people. When it is established for them, it is established for others, since there is no one who makes a distinction. If it is said: why can the intended meaning of the presentation of the Fire to them morning and evening not be the presentation of admonitions to them in the world? Because when the people of religion mention to them the promise and the warning and frighten them with the punishment of God, they have presented the Fire to them. We then say: there is in the verse what prevents taking it as the punishment of the grave, and its explanation is from two aspects. The first reading is the choice of Abu 'Ubaydah, who argued for it with His saying ﴿they are exposed﴾, meaning this is done to them, and so likewise (admit). As for the basis of the second reading, it is His saying ﴿Enter the gates of Hell﴾. Here ends the discussion of the story of the believer of the family of Pharaoh.

Know that when the discussion of that story led to explaining the conditions of the Fire, Allah therefore mentioned after it the story of the disputes that take place among the people of the Fire between the leaders and the followers. He said: ﴿And when they argue within the Fire﴾. The meaning is: mention, O Muhammad, to your people when they argue, that is, some of them dispute with others. Then he explained their dispute: the weak say to the leaders ﴿Indeed, we were your followers﴾ in the world. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "tabaʿan" is like khadam, the plural of khādim, or it is of the form dhawī tabaʿ, meaning followers, or it is a description with the verbal noun. ﴿So will you relieve us of a portion of the Fire?﴾ meaning: will you, O leaders, be able to ward off from us a portion of the punishment? Know that those followers know that those leaders have no power to grant that lightening, and their purpose in this speech is only to exaggerate in shaming those leaders and wounding their hearts, because they are the ones who strove to bring these followers into various kinds of misguidance. At this point the leaders say ﴿Indeed, we are all within it﴾, meaning that all of us are subject to this punishment, so if I were able to remove the punishment from you I would remove it from myself. Then they say: ﴿Indeed, Allah has judged between the servants﴾, meaning He conveys to each one the measure of his right of bliss or of punishment. At this point the followers despair of their leaders, so they return to the keepers of Hell and say to them: ﴿Call upon your Lord to lighten for us a day of the torment.﴾ If it is asked: why did He not say: "And those in the Fire said to its keepers," but rather said: ﴿And those in the Fire said to the keepers of Hell﴾? We say there are two answers:

The first: that the purpose of mentioning Hell is to magnify and make the matter terrible. The second: that Jahannam is the name of a place which is the deepest part of the Fire, from their saying: "a well jahannam," meaning of great depth, and in it are the greatest categories of disbelievers in punishment, and the keepers of that place will be the highest in rank among the keepers of Hell before Allah. When the disbelievers know that the matter is so, they seek help from them. Those angels say to them ﴿Did there not come to you your messengers with clear proofs?﴾ The point is that before the sending of messengers the people could say ﴿there came to us no bringer of good tidings or warner﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 19]. But after the coming of the messengers there remains no excuse or pretext, as He said: ﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15]. This verse indicates that obligation is not realized except after the coming of the law.

Then those angels say to the disbelievers: "Call upon Him yourselves, for we do not dare to do that, and we do not intercede except under two conditions: one of them is that the one for whom intercession is made is a believer, and the second is that permission for intercession has been given." Neither of these two conditions exists, so our undertaking this intercession is impossible. "But call upon Him yourselves." Their saying "Call" is not for hope of benefit, but to indicate disappointment, for if the near angel's supplication is not heard, how will the supplication of the disbelievers be heard? Then they openly tell them that their supplication has no effect, so they say ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is only in error.﴾ If it is said: need is impossible for God, and if that is so, it is impossible to say that He was harmed by these criminals because of their crime; and if being harmed is impossible for Him, then the desire for vengeance is impossible for Him. If this is established, we say: inflicting these great harms upon those disbelievers is harm with no benefit in it for God the Exalted nor for any of the servants. It is therefore harm empty of every beneficial aspect. How, then, is it fitting for the Merciful, the Generous, to keep that pain forever and ever, without having mercy on their need, without hearing their supplication, and without turning to their humility

Page 66
and brokenness? Even if the hardest-hearted of people did such torment to some of his servants, his generosity and mercy would invite him to pardon them, although this master is in the place of benefit, harm, and need. How, then, is such harm fitting for the Most Generous of the generous? We say: the acts of God are not subject to causal explanation, and "He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned" [al-Anbiya': 23]. So when the true judgment came regarding this in the true Book, it became obligatory to affirm it. And Allah knows best what is correct.

Hamzah read "ḥāqa" (حِيقَ) with a kasrah on the ḥāʾ, and so in every place in the Qur'an, while the rest read it with a fatḥah.

As for His saying ﴿The Fire—they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Our companions (the Ash'arites) used this verse to establish the punishment of the grave. They said: the verse requires that the Fire be presented to them morning and evening, and the intended meaning is not the Day of Resurrection, because He said: ﴿and on the Day the Hour will be established: "Admit the people of Pharaoh into the most severe torment."﴾ Nor is the intended meaning the worldly life, because the presentation of the Fire to them morning and evening did not occur in the world. Thus it is established that this presentation occurred after death and before the Day of Resurrection, and this indicates the establishment of the punishment of the grave for these people. When it is established for them, it is established for others, since there is no one who makes a distinction. If it is said: why can the intended meaning of the presentation of the Fire to them morning and evening not be the presentation of admonitions to them in the world? Because when the people of religion mention to them the promise and the warning and frighten them with the punishment of God, they have presented the Fire to them. We then say: there is in the verse what prevents taking it as the punishment of the grave, and its explanation is from two aspects. The first: that punishment must be constant and uninterrupted, while His saying ﴿they are exposed to it morning and evening﴾ implies that the punishment occurs only at these two times, so it is established that this cannot be taken as the punishment of the grave. The second: that morning and evening occur only in the world; in the grave there is no existence of them. Thus by these two aspects it is established that this verse cannot be taken as referring to the punishment of the grave.

The answer to the first question: in the world, words were presented to them that remind them of the matter of the Fire, not that the Fire itself was presented to them. So according to their view, the meaning of the verse becomes: the words reminding of the matter of the Fire were presented to them, and this leads to abandoning the apparent wording and turning to metaphor. As for his saying: the verse indicates the occurrence of this punishment at these two times, and that is not permissible, we say: why is it not permissible that it suffices in the grave to deliver the punishment to him at these two times, and then, at the establishment of the Resurrection, he is cast into the Fire, and his punishment continues after that? Also, it is not impossible that the mention of morning and evening is a metaphor for permanence, like His saying: ﴿And for them their provision therein morning and evening﴾. As for his saying that there is no morning and evening in the grave or in the Resurrection, we say: why is it not permissible to say that at the occurrence of these two times for the people of the world, the punishment is presented to them? And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 40, verses 53–55:**

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe, in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses stand,﴾ ﴿the Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers, and for them is the curse, and for them is the evil abode.﴾ ﴿And We certainly gave Moses guidance and caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Scripture,﴾ ﴿as guidance and reminder for those of understanding.﴾ ﴿So be patient; indeed, the promise of Allah is true. And ask forgiveness for your sin and exalt [Allah] with praise of your Lord in the evening and the morning.﴾

Know that there are several aspects to the arrangement (naẓm) of this passage. The first: when Allah mentioned His protection of Moses (peace be upon him) and that believing man from the plotting of Pharaoh, He clarified in this verse that He helps His messengers and those who believe with them. The second: when He had previously explained the disputes that occur among the people of the Fire, and that when they resort to the keepers of Hell they say, ﴿Did there not come to you your messengers with clear evidences?﴾ (Ghafir: 50), He followed this with mention of the messengers and that He helps them in this world and the Hereafter. The third, which is closest to me: the discourse at the beginning of the surah began with His words, ﴿None dispute in the verses of Allah except those who disbelieve, so let not their coming and going throughout the land deceive you﴾ (Ghafir: 4), and the discourse extended in refuting those disputers, and [showing] that the righteous are always occupied with repelling the schemes of the falsifiers. All of this Allah mentioned as consolation to the Messenger (ﷺ) and to make him patient in bearing the harm of his people.

When the discourse reached the ultimate level in establishing the matter sought, Allah promised His Messenger (ﷺ) that He would help him against his enemies in this world and in the Hereafter, and so He said: ﴿Indeed, We will surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾ to the end of the verse. As for this world, it is what is meant by His words, ﴿and he said, "Indeed, you have taken...﴾ and as for the Hereafter, it is what is meant by His words, ﴿and on the Day when the witnesses stand.﴾ So the sum of the discourse is that Allah promised that He will help the prophets and messengers, and He will help those who support them with a support whose effect appears in this world and in the Hereafter.

Know that Allah's support of the righteous is achieved in several ways. The first: support through proof (ḥujjah). Allah has called proof "authority" (sulṭān) in more than one place, and this support is general to all the righteous. How fitting is it that Allah named this support "authority," because worldly authority may vanish and may be replaced by poverty, humiliation, need and weakness; but the authority that comes through proof remains forever, and the intrusion of defect and weakness upon it is impossible.

The second: they are supported by praise and honour, for even if the oppressors overpower a person of the righteous, they cannot remove his praise from the tongues of the people.

The third: they are supported because their inner selves are filled with the lights of proof and the strength of certainty, for they look upon the oppressors and the ignorant as the angels of the heavens look upon the basest of things.

The fourth: even if the falsifiers happen to gain dominance over the righteous, in most cases this does not last; rather it becomes evident to the people that this was a matter that occurred contrary to what is obligatory and contrary to the truth.

The fifth: if the righteous happens to fall into some kind of feared harm, that becomes a cause of increased reward for him and elevation of his ranks. The sixth: the oppressors and falsifiers, just as they die, their traces die too, and no trace or report of them remains in the world. As for the righteous, their traces remain throughout time, people follow them in works of piety and goodness, and they leave [what is wrong] for the sake of their [the righteous's] gifts. All of this is kinds of Allah's support of the righteous in this world.

Know that the comprehensive aspects of acts of obedience are confined to two types: repentance from what is not fitting (tawbah), and occupation with what is fitting. The first is prior to the second in terms of inherent rank, so it is necessary that it be prior to it in mention. As for repentance from what is not fitting, it is His words: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin.﴾ Those who criticise the infallibility of the prophets (peace be upon them) cling to this, but we interpret it as repentance from leaving what is better and more excellent, or as referring to what proceeded from them before prophethood. It has also been said that what is intended by it is pure devotional worship (ta'abbud), as in His words: ﴿Our Lord, and give us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾ (Al 'Imran: 194), for granting that thing is obligatory, and then He commanded us to seek it; and as in His words: ﴿My Lord, judge with truth﴾ (al-Anbiya': 112), since we know that He judges only with truth. It has also been said that the verbal noun is an attribution to the agent and the object: so His words, ﴿and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ are of the type of the verbal noun attributed to the object, meaning: ask forgiveness for the sin of your community on your behalf.

As for occupation with what is fitting, it is His words: ﴿And exalt [Allah] with praise of your Lord in the evening and the morning.﴾ *Al-tasbīḥ* (glorification) is an expression for declaring Allah free from everything unbefitting to Him. *Al-'ashiyy* (the evening) and *al-ibkār* (the morning): it has been said they are the Asr prayer and the Fajr prayer. It has also been said: *al-ibkār* is an expression for the beginning of the day until midday, and *al-'ashiyy* is an expression for midday until the end of the day, so every time is included in it. It has been said that what is meant is the two extremes of the day, as He said: ﴿And establish prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ (Hud: 114). In sum, what is meant by it is the command to be constant in remembrance of Allah, that the tongue not slacken in it, and that the heart not be heedless of it, until a person by this means enters the company of the angels, as He said describing them: ﴿They glorify [Him] night and day; they do not slacken﴾ (al-Anbiya': 20). And Allah knows best.

Know that when God, exalted is He, had made clear that the claim of the Resurrection is true and certain, and since it is known necessarily that a person will benefit on the Day of Resurrection only through obedience to God, exalted is He, occupation with obedience is necessarily among the most important matters. And since the noblest kinds of obedience are supplication (du'a') and humble entreaty, God, exalted is He, commanded it in this verse, saying: **"Your Lord says: 'Call upon Me, and I will respond to you.'"** People differed about the meaning of His words **"call upon Me."** It was said that it is a command to supplicate. It was also said that it is a command to worship, based on His words after it: **"those who are too proud to worship Me."** Were it not that the command to supplicate is a command to worship in general, the words **"Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me"** would have no meaning. Also, du'a' in the sense of worship is frequent in the Qur'an, as in His words: **"They call upon none besides Him but females"** (4:117).

It is answered that du'a' is an acknowledgment of servanthood, lowliness and neediness. So it is as if it were said: the one who abandons supplication only abandons it because he is too proud to display servanthood. As for the claim that du'a' in the sense of worship is frequent in the Qur'an, it is answered that abandoning the apparent meaning is not resorted to except with a separate proof.

If it is asked: how did He say **"call upon Me, and I will respond to you"** when many people call upon Him and are not answered? Al-Ka'bi answered this by saying: supplication is valid only on a condition, and whoever supplicates under that condition is answered. That condition is that what is sought through supplication be a benefit and a wisdom. Then he asked himself: "But what if He does what is better without supplication? Then what is the benefit of supplication?"

He answered this in two ways. The first: in it there is the anxiety and the turning to God. The second: this also applies to everything. For if He knows that He will do it, then He must do it, so there is no benefit in supplication; and if He knows that He will not do it, then He certainly will not do it, so there is no benefit in supplication. Everything they say here is our answer as well. This is the full extent of what he mentioned. But I have another view on this, which is that He said: **"call upon Me, and I will respond to you."** So whoever calls upon God while there is in his heart a grain of reliance on his wealth, his rank, his relatives, his friends, his good fortune and his striving, then in reality he has not called upon God except with his tongue. As for his heart, he is relying on someone other than God to attain that sought object. Such a person has not called upon his Lord at any time. But if he calls upon Him at a time when no attention to anything other than God remains in his heart, then it is apparent that the response is attained. If you understand this, then in it there is complete good news: the heart's total severance from everything other than God does not occur except near death, for a person is then certain that nothing will benefit him except the grace of God, exalted is He. So according to the principle we have mentioned, supplication at that time must be accepted by God. We hope, by the grace and kindness of God, that He will grant us success in supplication joined with sincerity and humble entreaty at that time. Know that the thorough discussion of supplication has already been mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah.

* * *

Then God, exalted is He, said: **"Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humbled."** That is, abased. This is a great kindness from God, exalted is He, in that He mentioned a severe threat for abandoning supplication. If it is said: it is narrated from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that he said, relating from the Lord of Might, that He said: "Whoever is occupied by remembering Me from asking Me, I will give him the best of what I give to those who ask." This report implies that abandoning supplication is better, while this verse indicates that abandoning supplication entails a severe threat. How then can the two be reconciled? We say: there is no doubt that if the intellect is absorbed in praise, that is more excellent than supplication, because supplication includes knowledge of the might of lordship and the lowliness of servanthood.

Then God, exalted is He, said: **"It is God who made the night for you to rest in."** Know that its connection to what precedes it is in two ways. The first: it is as if He, exalted is He, said: I bestowed upon you before your request these great and magnificent blessings, and whoever bestowed such lofty blessings before a request, how would He not bestow lesser things after a request? The second: when He commanded supplication, it is as if it were said: occupation with supplication must necessarily be preceded by the attainment of knowledge. So what is the proof of the existence of the capable God? God, exalted is He, has mentioned these ten proofs of His existence, power and wisdom. Know that we have explained that the proofs of the existence and power of God are either celestial or elemental. As for the celestial ones, they are many kinds, the first of which is the alternation of night and day.
